speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table today the Main Estimates for 1987-88, this being the third set of Estimates that I have presented on behalf of the government. These Main Estimates, which amount to $110.1 billion in budgetary spending, are yet another example of the success of our sustained efforts to curb uncontrolled growth in public spending.
I have also tabled today a special Supplementary Estimate for 1987-88 in the amount of $700 million, to provide for the balance of the payments committed to grain farmers under the special Canadian Grains Program. This item was specifically not included in these Main Estimates because the government has undertaken to disburse this money well before full supply will be available on these Main Estimates. The Supplementary Estimate will provide for appropriate parliamentary review as well as the voting of full supply on this item by the end of this month.

March 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
Mr. Speaker, the 1987-88 budgetary Main Estimates are 2.9 per cent higher than those tabled for 1986-87. However, you will recall that when I tabled the 1986-87 Main Estimates last year, I pointed out that a $500 million expenditure reduction, announced by the Minister of Finance the day before in his Budget, was not reflected in those Estimates. Thus, after making an adjustment for this item, as well as for the increase in the special Canadian Grains Programs, the year-over-year growth in these Main Estimates amounts to 3.8 per cent, slightly lower than last year, lower than the rate of inflation, and lower than it has been since 1962.
[DOT] (mo)

This marks the third year in succession that this Government has tabled a set of Main Estimates where the growth rate has declined. No Government has been able to make this claim in almost two decades. We can be justifiably proud of this record as it demonstrates clearly our sustained commitment to controlling spending and reducing the deficit.
The extent of this commitment is illustrated by an examination of major elements of these Main Estimates. Seventy-two billion, three hundred million dollars representing two-thirds of the total, will be spent on statutory programs; that is, spending governed by separate legislation. They include, for example, payments to the elderly by Health and Welfare Canada which will amount to some $14.6 billion in 1987-88, the largest single item in these Estimates next to the public debt charges. They also include family allowances, the Canada Assistance Plan, fiscal transfers to the provinces, municipal grants, and a variety of agricultural and transportation subsidies. Over all, statutory estimates are $2.8 billion, or 4 per cent, higher than last year. The remaining $37.8 billion, or one-third of total Main Estimates, represent expenditures which Parliament will be asked explicitly to authorize for the upcoming year.
The Government can in general exercise greater discretion over these latter voted expenditures. Indeed, it is this category of spending on which Government has focused many of its expenditure restraint measures. As a result, the annual increase in the voted portion of Main Estimates will be 3.4 per cent over last year. This is the third year in a row in which this growth rate has been less than inflation. Over the past three years the rate of growth has averaged only 1.3 per cent. This is the best performance since the three-year period at the beginning of the 1960s.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Despite this continued commitment to expenditure restraint the Government has made provision in these Estimates for increases to such important priorities as programs for aboriginal peoples, veterans, defence, external affairs and foreign aid. Included in these Main Estimates is some $2 billion to fund programs for our aboriginal people in such areas as education, social development, capital facilities and community services. In addition, $700 million is to be transferred to the territorial Governments to assist them in providing services to residents of the North. Veterans' pensions
and allowances and health services purchased on behalf of veterans amount to $1.4 billion in these Main Estimates. The increase in the Main Estimates allocations for these social programs total almost $300 million, an increase of over 7 per cent from a year ago. There is also significant growth in external affairs and aid expenditures, reflecting increases in bilateral development assistance, increases in payments to international financial institutions, and contributions towards the cost of development assistance undertakings by Canadian and international non-governmental organizations. Altogether the increase in voted estimates for these activities is $290 million, or 10.6 per cent.
The Main Estimates allocation for defence is $10.3 billion, 92 per cent of which is voted expenditures. This portion is fully one-quarter of the total voted estimates. Personnel costs represent about 44 per cent of defence spending, with another quarter of the defence budget earmarked for capital spending for such items as the CF-18 fighter aircraft, the Canadian patrol frigate, the North American air defence modernization, and the Tribal Class update and modernization programs. Over-all spending on defence, external affairs and aid increases by over $700 million in these Main Estimates, reflecting the priority assigned to international commitments in these areas. These increases in priority areas of spending have been achieved through internal reallocation which has allowed the Government to limit the growth rate in voted appropriations to 3.4 per cent for 1987-88.

As Hon. Members are aware, Mr. Speaker, prudent fiscal planning requires that a government set aside reserves within its overall fiscal plan to accommodate unanticipated requirements that may arise in the course of the year. To the extent these reserves are allocated, they will appear in the form of Supplementary Estimates items which are presented to Parliament for review and approval. As part of its restraint effort, the government has reduced and more rigorously controlled access to the reserves set aside for contingency purposes. The impact of this will be demonstrated later this week when I table the final Supplementary Estimates for 1986-87. At that time it will be noted that total Supplementary Estimates for the current year will amount to less than 2 per cent of 1986-87 Main Estimates-the lowest percentage since 1968-69.
Members will recall that from the very beginning this government has committed itself to the pursuit of productive management in the federal public sector. Disciplined management has been a consistent theme of the government's various restraint measures and Budget statements. Through the introduction of productive management policies and actions we have sought to create an environment and institutional momentum within the Public Service which stress efficiency, innovation and value for money in the delivery of federal programs and services.
March 2, 1987

The fruit of these efforts are reflected in the 1987-88 Main Estimates, Mr. Speaker. An examination of the payment distribution of these Estimates shows that the non-defence operating and capital spending is marginally lower in the 1987-88 Main Estimates than it was in 1984-85. Taking inflation into account, this is a reduction of just over 12 per cent over this period.
This is a significant achievement, Mr. Speaker, especially if one notes that spending on wages and salaries, the major portion of these costs, is in large part governed by collective agreements, and that the increased costs of negotiated wage settlements have averaged approximately 3.5 per cent per annum. I might also note that the open approach taken by this government to labour relations in the Public Service, including the introduction of Master Agreements and the negotiation of responsible and fair wage settlements, has greatly facilitated the government's efforts to contain expenditures while maintaining essential services to the public. These efforts have also meant that Public Service managers are being continually challenged to deliver government programs with fewer human and financial resources, and to accommodate and expanding clientele and rising workload through efficiency gains, productivity improvements and imaginative use of alternative production and delivery techniques.
I just mentioned that public service managers are employing fewer human resources in program operations. You will recall that in his May, 1985, Budget statement, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced the Government's intention to reduce the size of the public service by 15,000 person-years over five years beginning with the 1986-87 fiscal year. Consistent with this commitment, the 1986-87 Main Estimates tabled last year showed a reduction of some 5,500 person years compared to the previous year. The Main Estimates I tabled today show a further reduction of almost 3,100 person-years. I can therefore report that the Government is squarely on track in achieving its five-year target with more than half of the planned reductions already obtained.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Indeed, measured on a comparable basis, the number of authorized person-years reported in these Main Estimates is the lowest since the 1980-81 Estimates. With the completion of this program in 1990-91 the number of person-years will be comparable to that of pre-1975 levels.
At the same time the Government's innovative work force adjustment policy, strengthened in 1985 in consultation with the public service unions, has been vigorously applied in a concerted effort to minimize the impact on individual employees affected by the person year reduction measures. In
Statements by Ministers
May, 1986, I announced that the Government was confident that the majority of affected employees could be redeployed within the public service. I also forecast that no more than 500 public service employees would be laid off as a result of the first year of the person-year reductions. With the fiscal year drawing to an end, I remain confident as to the accuracy of that forecast. I will be reporting more fully to Parliament when the final results are available in April. Hon. Members can be assured that the same strong effort to minimize layoffs will continue throughout 1987-88 and in future years.
I have referred in my remarks to the notable contribution made by public service managers to the Government's restraint efforts. When I tabled the 1986-87 Main Estimates last year I stated that a productivity bonus was being developed as a new feature of the Government's management compensation package. Such a feature would serve to reward managers for meeting or exceeding expenditure reduction targets while still achieving their other program and policy goals. A final decision on implementation of the productivity bonus had obviously to wait for an assessment of 1986-87 performance.
As the Minister of Finance reported in his Budget last month, the Government's record on expenditure management has been exceptional. The full $500 million expenditure reduction announced in the February, 1986, Budget has been identified and implemented. As I have already noted, person-year reduction goals have been fully achieved and, in some cases, are ahead of schedule. Steady progress has been made in other key government initiatives such as improved cash management, increased cost recovery, continued privatization of Crown corporations, and reduced overhead and administrative costs.
The Treasury Board has concluded that senior public service managers have been instrumental in the realization of these improvements and has approved a productivity bonus for its senior management of from 1 to 1.5 per cent of salary for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1987. The total estimated cost of this bonus is $4.5 million.

To further demonstrate its commitment to management excellence, the Treasury Board has also authorized an increase, to $10,000, of the maximum value of the Outstanding Achievement Award. This Award, which consists of a citation and a Canadian work of art, can be given annually to up to five senior level public servants who are selected by a six-member panel of Canadians appointed from outside the Public Service. The award was first introduced in 1966. The increase in this award is another clear signal of the importance the government attaches to fostering and rewarding exceptional performance by Public Service managers.

March 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Main Estimates tabled today represent a further significant contribution to the government's record on expenditure management.
First, this is the third consecutive year that the growth rate in Main Estimates has declined. Second, the rate of growth in 1987-88 Main Estimates is the lowest increase in 20 years. Third, the size of the Public Service in 1987-88 will be at its lowest level since 1980-81.

In summary, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Main Estimates tabled today represent a further significant contribution to the Government's record on expenditure management. This is the third consecutive year that the growth rate in Main Estimates has declined. Second, the rate of growth in the 1987-88 Main Estimates is the lowest increase in a quarter century. Finally, the size of the public service in 1987-88 will be at its lowest level since 1980-81.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: This track record clearly reflects the Government's strong commitment to sound management and to the operation of an efficient and effective public service while maintaining and expanding programs which serve the real needs of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us start at the Minister's last point; that is, the bribery payments. Let us start with the new system which the Government has brought in, effective March 31, to pay $4.5 million to senior public servants. According to the Minister, it is for good management in cutting back person years and keeping expenditures down. What is the job of these senior public servants and why are they being paid, if not for good management? The definition of senior management is everyone from the Deputy Minister down. The Government says there is some $4.5 million and, presumably at the end of the month, it will issue cheques up to 1 per cent and 1.5 per cent of the levels. That means the top of the salary scale to which that manager is entitled.
[DOT] (U30)

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: What does that mean?

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
The Hon. Member asks what that means. I do not suppose anyone knows what it means, but the managers will know when they receive their hand delivered cheques. They will receive $1,000 or $1,500 for ensuring that person years are reduced, according to the Minister.
It is no wonder that the Government exceeded its predicted lay-offs of 2,500 this coming year. It is eliminating 3,100 person years. There are well paid employees in our society who are receiving cash bonuses for eliminating people in jobs on the lower end of the income scale.
The Government brags about the elimination of 3,100 people. If the Minister read the mail we are receiving concerning this matter he would know that people are being laid off throughout the country, with no job prospects in the private sector. People who have 25 years experience in the public service are being laid off with the stroke of a pen. Those people know as a result of this announcement that they are being laid off because a senior manager will receive a lump sum payment at the end of this month as a result of that lay-off.
This incredible system which the Government brags about affects engineers who are being laid off in Public Works, employees in the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans, people who work in employment offices across the country and those at the scientific research group at the Bedford Institute which will be closed at the end of this month. Someone will receive a $1,000 cheque at the end of the month for accomplishing these lay-offs.
There will be an average payment of $1,000 to highly paid public servants, including Deputy Ministers, at the end of this month. This $4.5 million in bribe payments will result in some 6,000 cheques being issued. One wonders what country would follow such a plan. Obviously the Treasury Board had quite a problem devising the guidelines because it had no other country to use as a model. The system announced by the Minister today does not exist in any other democratic country. We believe these payments are being made for a job that the managers were supposed to do in the first place. We regard it simply as bribery cheques being paid to managers in the public service in this country.
The Minister's statement could be summed up by saying that he is trying to give Canadians the impression that government spending is down. Yet spending has risen considerably. When the Government took office it assumed a national debt of approximately $189 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is predicting that national debt to be up to $300 billion this year. Governments of Canada built an accumulated debt of some $189 billion since Confederation, but this Government has increased that debt to $300 billion in some two years.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
The truth hurts, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Finance said that while spending is up, revenues have also increased. Government revenues have increased to match the increases in the selective spending the Government has undertaken. Recently a Cabinet Minister stated: "-they were only within 10 per cent of the lowest bid and I directed the contract to go to them because they were from my province".
Not all of the information is contained in the Estimates tabled today. We learned that lesson last week when we discovered that a $1 million cheque was given to the County of Pictou in Nova Scotia to build a courthouse. That grant does not come under any federal government program.
March 2, 1987

Every tendering process includes a stipulation that the contract will not necessarily be given to the lowest bidder. The Government should come clean and delete the word "necessarily" so that the stipulation states that the contract will not be given to the lowest bidder. We have seen the Government awarding contracts not only to the second lowest bidder, but the third, fourth and so on.
People should not only concern themselves with the small contracts that are awarded throughout the country, because there are large government contracts being made available and we can see where the money is being spent.
It is true that revenues are up. Last Sunday on CTV's Question Period, the Minister of Finance was asked a question by Mr. John Ferguson in which he said:
I think that the figures from the Fraser Institute in Vancouver suggest that you have been the taxingest Finance Minister in history, that taxes have gone up more, personal income taxes have gone up more under your period of finance than in any other period.
The Minister responded:
What we have been doing here, John-
Referring to John Ferguson, the writer:
-is to bring the level of taxation back to where it had been in the middle 1970s. Previous Ministers of Finance had let go of the tax reins and the level of taxation as a per cent of income had gone down and down-
Who are these former Ministers of Finance whom the Minister said let go of the tax reins in the mid-1970s? The Minister says we must grab the tax reins and bring taxes to their levels before the mid-1970s and make people pay through their taxes. It is as if former Tory Finance Ministers from 20 or 30 years ago are saying: "To you we throw the reins of taxation. Be yours to hold them high". That is why revenues are up in this expenditure package, as well as expenditures.
How does the Minister take hold of those tax reins? He taxes potato chips, corn and cheese-based puffs, brittle pretzels, salted nuts, popcorn, granola bars, frozen snacks, popsicles and ice cream bars. That is what the Minister of Finance does to grab the reins of taxation, to rein in the taxes from the ordinary people of Canada. And who does he pick on? He picks on children. There never was such a tax prior to the 1970s. The Minister of Finance is reining in his taxes from the children.
My Party, the Official Opposition, and I find the Minister of Finance to be way off track in his priorities on taxation. The Minister who tabled the Estimates here today is just as much off track in offering a bonus to public servants and bragging about 3,100 people being laid off. We find it passing strange that Departments such as the Department of Fisheries and Oceans should have a continual decrease in funds since the Government took office. It is down to $551 million this year. Other Government Departments have followed the same route. We have seen, on the other hand, the Government toss money at the Prime Minister's Office to increase his number of staff, and to the Ministers of this Government so they can have all
Statements by Ministers
the staff they want to award contracts, not to the lowest bidder but to the second and third highest bidder, and to give special grants for their own pet projects in their own constituencies which do not come under any program.
Where were the increases in these Estimates today? They were very markedly in the Prime Minister's Office and the Office of the Privy Council. When we look at the percentages we wonder in what direction the Government is going. I am sure the general public will look at the Budget and these Estimates and see we have slight increases in the expenditures of Departments of the federal Government, but they will also see the 18.9 per cent increase in the Budget of the Department of External Affairs for last year and a 15.6 per cent increase this year, amounting to over $3 billion. They will also see family allowances under these Estimates held down to their expenditures and the cuts made to reduce it by three percentage points. They will ask where the equality is of having the budget of the Department of External Affairs 50 per cent higher than the entire budget for family allowances. They will wonder where the justice is behind these kinds of Estimates. The Government will not last its entire term after tabling Estimates such as these.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88 STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on these Estimates. A year ago when the Estimates came down I said that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Government had produced another set of spending Estimates which would suit Wall Street and Bay Street and, in the words of Ronald Reagan, "There you go again", because that is exactly what we have again this year. These Estimates indicate that the Government intends to continue pleasing the bond market, the financiers and the investment analysts, but it does not relate to the real situation Canadians face.
May I say in parenthesis, Madam Speaker, that I feel extremely distressed at suggestions just made by my hon. colleague from the Liberal Party that his Party is no longer committed to foreign aid. It is an important service and Canadians are prepared to share some of the wealth we have in our country in addition to giving justice to our own people. We can, I believe, do both.
I want to point out to the President of the Treasury Board, and to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), what we pointed out two weeks before the House rose for a week at the time of the Budget debate, that over the course of the past year, between January 1986 and January 1987, we have had an increase of 132,000 jobs in Ontario and an increase of only 5,000 jobs in the rest of the country. At the present moment there are 1.25 million Canadians out of work. It was clear from the Budget and clearer still from these Estimates that the Government has no strategy and no intention to do anything about that particular problem.
Regional Development spending is down by $3 billion from the year the Conservatives came to office. That has meant cuts in transportation, in the fisheries, in agriculture, apart from
3694

March 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
the special grains program, cuts in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. In fact there has been a further $1 billion taken out of DRIE in order to pay for the special grains project.
The Government is fighting the deficit this year on the backs of the unemployed and on the backs of the provinces. I remind the President of the Treasury Board and his colleagues that today there are seven provinces which have unemployment rates higher than at the time of the height of the recession in 1981-82. Yet the fact is that the moneys which are being transferred to the provinces are not going to the provinces with the greatest unemployment rates but to the Province of Ontario. Of the total amounts going to the provinces, in terms of tax payments and transfer payments, a total increase of $550 million is going to that poor suffering Province of Ontario. It is a good province which I represent. However, in southern Ontario there has been some economic recovery, and Ontario receives $550 million compared to the $600 million which will go to nine other provinces.

And in particular, Madam Speaker, I want to stress the fact that the Province of Quebec is especially hard hit by the Government cut-backs with respect to transfer payments and payments in terms of tax point transfers. Madam Speaker, we can see that despite the fact that the unemployment rate in Quebec is about 10.8 per cent, the increase in these equalization or transfer payments to Quebec amounts to only $7 million, up 0.1 per cent. By comparison, Ontario's unemployment rate is 6.6 per cent, yet the province will benefit from an increase in equalization and fiscal transfer payments of $50 million, up 7 per cent.

Where are the priorities of the Government which would permit that kind of situation and then turn around to the Province of Quebec and tell it, as it has as recently as the last couple of weeks, that the federal Government is not prepared to deal on the same basis with equalization with Quebec relative to other provinces which received certain forms of revenue guarantees.
Manitoba has an unemployment rate of 7.9 per cent. It will receive an increase of only $1 million or a 0.1 per cent increase in terms of payments for post-secondary education, hospital insurance, medicare and its general transfers which come from the Government of Canada. British Columbia, which has an unemployment rate of 13.8 per cent at the end of January, will see an increase of only 2 per cent in terms of the payments under the shared cost programs with respect to fiscal transfers from the Government.
I want to say that the priorities of the Government are reflected not just in these Estimates but in what is happening on the tax side. The Government has played around with a little here and a little less there in terms of spending estimates. At the same time since the Conservatives came to power they
have increased personal and sales tax revenues from individuals by 52 per cent and have decreased corporate tax revenues by 18 per cent. That is despite a very sharp increase anticipated this coming year in terms of corporate profits. Those are the priorities of the Government.

Another point I want to emphasize, Madam Speaker, is that in these estimates the Government has decided to consolidate the unemployment insurance fund accounts. Indeed the Government sees this as a way to show that unemployment insurance benefits paid to Canada's unemployed come from all Canadians, while in fact it is an insurance fund from which Canadian men and women are entitled to draw benefits if they are out of work, if they suffer from the economic policies of this Government. But at the same time as it consolidates the unemployment insurance fund accounts, Madam Speaker, it is not doing anything to make sure that the estimates will cover payments for tax expenditures.
According to the Auditor General, tax expenditures are estimated at about $30 billion a year. But in spite of that we have no idea which companies will get these huge payments. Who will benefit from these payments? There is no indication whatsoever in the Government estimates.
On the one hand the unemployed are included in such a way that if the Conservatives were to stay in power-which is very unlikely-then they would begin to take away unemployment payments directly from the unemployed. That is the reason the Government has consolidated these accounts. On the other hand, the Conservatives refuse to put in any listing at all of the tax expenditures which are benefiting, in the main, large corporations and wealthy Canadians.
I note that the Government has left a substantial chunk of $2.4 billion for pre-election hand-outs to be made over the course of the fall and next spring.
In terms of priorities, the Government is decreasing corporate tax and increasing personal tax because of its priorities, while doing nothing about tax expenditures which are so costly to Canadians.
I represent a Public Service riding. Once again, public servants will be distressed over the news received in this year's Estimates. Some 3,000 jobs will be cut despite the assurances of the President of the Treasury Board. This means that individuals will be disrupted and forced to move from one community to another in order to save their jobs. They will be pressured out of the Public Service by means of various golden handshakes and other inducements which they will be given. Some of them will, as a number did last year, become too discouraged and will go down on the Treasury Board's lists as being no longer interested in government employment. They
March 2, 1987

are no longer interested because of the nature of the employment they will be offered and because of the adjustments to which they will be compelled to adjust.
If the Government insists on achieving this down-sizing of Government it can and should be achieved without any individual public servant being forced to lose his or her job. If it were possible again to manage it to the point at which only a few hundred people will be fired, as happened last year, then the statement I made last year that no civil servant need ever lose his or her job could have been amply fulfilled for the expenditure of perhaps $4.5 million. That is the sum which is being given as a bonus to senior managers in the Public Service for their work in cutting and chopping heads in the departments for which they are responsible. I suggest that the President of the Treasury Board stand up now and undertake that not one single man or woman working for the people of Canada will be compelled to leave his or her job. That would be a change of heart for the Government which now has a heartless policy of wanting to show the people on St. James Street and Bay Street a few limp, wretched bodies of public servants who have been forced to walk the plank.
Once again this year I asked Treasury Board officials what proportion of the 3,000 people who are to be displaced will be women. I asked what measures will be taken to monitor the situation to ensure that women and minority groups are not further disadvantaged by these cuts. I raised this same question during the response to the Estimates last year and no response was given at that time. I have not received a response this year either. I have been told that they will try to get the figures to me later today. But they do not have the figures because there is no awareness of the fact that women employees are particularly vulnerable to these cuts. There is no awareness and no program to ensure that not just scientists and senior managers will receive extra training or placement in order to save their jobs, but that secretaries, clerks and people doing important support jobs for the Government will also have access to the same type of retraining opportunities. Then they too should be able to save their jobs. They should not be forced out of the Public Service by means of what the Government is doing right now.

Madam Speaker, I should like to add a congratulatory note and point out the fact that, despite the 1985-86 cut-backs, the Government is still on the right track in terms of payments and budgetary estimates concerning funds available for foreign aid.

In terms of foreign aid, there has been a substantial increase this year. As a New Democrat, and I think Canadians will agree with me, I believe that Canada can and should be playing a very vigorous role in terms of providing aid to Latin America, Africa and Asia. We can do that and also do justice
Statements by Ministers
to people in depressed regions suffering from high unemployment. We can and should have a full employment policy. We are not doing justice to Canadians; but we should not seek to do justice to Canadians by doing injustice to people in the Third World.
I note the continued confusion of the Government with respect to Canada Post. I welcome the fact that it has drawn in its horns, to some extent. I deplore the fact that the Government has dithered now for a year and a half in terms of coming up with a clear policy. Canadians want to be assured of adequate postal services. That is a priority which comes before the need to reduce the postal deficit, if those are the choices which are to be put forward.
Once again the Government has cut funding for the Canadian Jobs Strategy at a time when we have 1.25 million unemployed. The Government has cut $154 million from its payment to the Jobs Strategy after having cut $100 million one year ago. I note a cut of over $100 million in payments for the loans and investments under Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is a sign that the Government lacks a real commitment in terms of adequate social housing.
Under regional expansion and investment the Government has cut $50 million from the Cape Breton Development Corporation, presumably because of its great success, a success about which the people of Cape Breton are certainly not aware. The Government's commitment in terms of economic development is so strong that, apart from the Defence Industry Productivity Program, it has cut the available funds through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
The Government has come up with an increase of 2.5 per cent in funding for the National Research Council, which brings the total up to about $400 million, down by $100 million from two-and-one-half years ago. That is how the Government has so miserably fulfilled the promises it made at the time of the 1984 election. It promised then that Canada should be a world leader in terms of research and development and in terms of science and technology.
I conclude by pointing this out.

The unemployment rate in this country is nearly 10 per cent, and 1,250,000 Canadian men and women are unemployed. The Government's policy seems to be to go on tolerating an intolerable situation where the unemployment rate will remain above 9 per cent across this country and, in some provinces, will be even higher than during the 1981-82 recession.

speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (for the Minister of Transport) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-39, an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act and the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Madam Speaker, indeed it is a pleasure to speak on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), who is gainfully employed otherwise in parliamentary business on the West
Coast today, on third reading stage of Bill C-39. As Your Honour said, this is an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act, and the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act in consequence thereof.
The Canada Shipping Act is the principal legislation covering the shipping activities of foreign ships in Canadian waters and Canadian ships anywhere in the world. It is primarily concerned with safety of life at sea and protection of the marine environment.
Improved safety is a major objective of the Government. It is recognized, for the first time, in the new National Transportation Act which has just been referred to the Standing Committee on Transport. The Government has introduced many measures for the safety of the travelling public. To name a few, the Aeronautics Act was amended in 1985, and regulations on the transport of dangerous goods were implemented in the same year. A national safety code is included in the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which is now before the House. As Hon. Members know, rail safety legislation is under development, and legislation for a multimodal accident investigation board is being seriously considered. The Bill respecting the Canada Shipping Act is another piece of the comprehensive plan for safety in the transportation system. Hon. Members will recall that the Bill was introduced in the House in the fall of 1985, and that debate on it was ongoing when the House recessed in June and subsequently prorogued in August last year. At that time the Bill was known as Bill C-75.
I believe the purpose of the Bill was supported by all Parties in the House, that is, safety at sea. However, the mechanism of cost recovery was not supported. The Bill before us now does not include the cost recovery clause.
Hear, hear!

Bill C-75 was extensively discussed at second reading stage in the House of Commons and in the legislative committee. I compliment the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth- Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), who really had the carriage of the Bill before the legislative committee. I also compliment several members of the Opposition, including primarily the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) and the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), on their very active and constructive interventions at the time. They were very vigorous in their presentations before the legislative committee. It was very interesting to be a part of that process. I compliment that committee and of course its chairperson, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), who discharged his very challenging task with unexpected and imaginative decorum.
In this complimentary stage, I also compliment the House Leaders for agreeing to the present House order so that a Bill which had received many hours of debate at second reading and before the legislative committee did not die with the
March 2, 1987

prorogation of Parliament. In effect there was an agreement to bring it back to the House, basically with the removal of Clause 4, so that we could give the Bill third reading and have it passed. I compliment the House Leaders for that agreement. As a result we have third reading stage today.
The matter has been extensively discussed. Over 60 witnesses representing 28 associations and organizations presented briefs to the legislative committee. More than 20 amendments were made to the Bill as originally introduced. As a result of the committee's work, I believe the Bill has been improved and will go a long way, in an era of advancing marine technology, to keeping Canada in the forefront of maritime and marine safety. Those amendments are an indication that the Government and government Members have listened to the constructive suggestions as reflected in the legislation now before the House.
I should now like to comment on some of the important features of the Bill relating to safety and the protection of the environment. During committee hearings the exclusion clause in respect of Canadian mobile offshore drilling units, also known as MODUs, was removed. The Bill now provides that regulations covering certain certification and training, design and construction, and accident prevention for MODUs, when submitted for Governor in Council approval, will be jointly recommended by the Minister of Transport and by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. There is precedent for the interesting innovation of a joint recommendation by two Ministers in Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. While it is an innovative procedure, it is an interim solution, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) is considering measures pertaining to mobile offshore drilling units. Hon. Members will recall the omnibus Bill respecting MODUs which was recommended by the royal commission investigation of the Ocean Ranger marine disaster.
Bill C-39 will permit the strengthening of Canadian participation within the international maritime organization and the international shipping community. It will allow Canada to accede to six international conventions and five codes dealing with the certification of masters and seamen, ship constructions, tonnage measurement, liability and compensation, and prevention and control of pollution from ships. The most important conventions are those relating to the standards of training, certification, and watch-keeping for seafarers; the convention for the prevention of pollution from ships, MARPOL; the associated conventions on civil liability for oil pollution damage and for the establishment of an international fund for compensation for oil pollution damage. The codes will also deal with construction and equipment for liquefied gas carriers, chemical carriers, mobile offshore drilling units, and the safety of dynamically supported craft. As you can see, Madam Speaker, the Bill is an omnibus Bill, covering all these areas which can potentially create many problems in the sea.
Penalties for oil pollution will be increased. Existing penalties of $100,000 will be increased to $200,000 and, for
Canada Shipping Act
contravening the regulations prohibiting the discharge of pollutants, the penalty will be increased from $100,000 to $250,000. The present penalty for a master who does not give reasonable assistance to a pollution prevention officer will be increased to $10,000 from the present $5,000 in the old Bill.
The Bill also revises and improves the scheme for liability and compensation for oil pollution damage. It will allow small claimants, such as fishermen and small boat operators whose property is damaged by oil pollution, to claim directly against our own domestic ship source oil pollution fund without having first to claim against shipowners, as is now the case. This will help eliminate lengthy and costly legal proceedings which now face many small claimants.
I should like to talk about certification of pleasure craft operators for a moment. It appears that members of the boating public and various boating associations believe that certification would be introduced for all types of pleasure craft. I should like to stress that this is not the case, again as a result of the very vigorous debate of the issue in the legislative committee.
In order to reassure the boating public, and in response to concerns expressed by Members and the general public, the Bill has been amended to exempt pleasure yachts of less than 20 metres, and vessels, boats, and craft of any length which are propelled manually by oars or paddles. This gets away from the interesting original interpretation of the definition that one might require certification of a rowing shell. Certainly that was never the intent of the legislators, even though it may have fallen within the imagination of the interpreters. Our intention here to is to clarify the issue of operator licensing for small pleasure craft and at the same time to provide enabling legislation which would allow the Government to respond to future certification requirements because of the size and power of the yachts involved.
I should now like to discuss the most controversial item in the Bill. Clause 4 deals with charges relating to navigational services. As the Minister has mentioned several times, the desirability of putting in place the important safety provisions contained in the Bill have led the Minister to withdraw the cost-recovery clause and re-introduce this legislation. This does not mean, however, that the Government has abandoned its commitment to deficit reduction of which the cost-recovery provisions of the Bill were an integral part. We continue to believe that the users of the Department's facilities and services including those provided by the Coast Guard should pay for a fair share of those incurred costs.
The Minister has accordingly instructed his Departmental officials to consult all interested parties on the principles that should govern the cost-recovery process and on the ways in which these principles could be implemented. The results of this consultation will be reported to the Minister and will be used as the basis for a return to Cabinet for approval to proceed with new enabling legislation for the introduction of

March 2, 1987
Canada Shipping Act
charges for services provided by the Coast Guard. It will have to return to the House at some time depending upon consultation and depending upon final agreement and/or the Cabinet's decision.
I think the Government has given proof of its willingness to listen to representations made by witnesses and by all committee members and to react to these representations in a most positive and constructive way. Members of all Parties will understand the importance of this legislation to the shipping community and to shipping activities in Canada. This Bill significantly improves and modernizes a 50-year-old Act that dates back to 1936.
I urge Hon. Members to consider the important safety features which are fundamental to the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act and to recognize the improvements that have been made in this legislation as a result of this Bill. Therefore, in the interests of marine safety, I ask in the name of the Minister that this House give expeditious passage to this legislation which has been long awaited both nationally and internationally.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise again to participate in the debate on this Bill. In fact, the last time I had the opportunity to participate in the debate on this Bill it was entitled Bill C-75. At the end of last June, as I recall, I was about seven hours into my speech and was just warming up on the measure called Clause 4, that Draconian clause, when the Speaker, not intentionally I am sure, rose to his feet to inform us that the House was rising for the summer. Unfortunately for the Government, fortunately for the marine industry of Canada, the result of the interruption by the Speaker of my speech, which I now hope to continue today, was that the Bill was lost and had to be re-introduced.
I enjoy hearing from the gentleman who has just spoken. He is a very able Chairman of the Transport Committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Should have been a Minister.

He should have been a Minister of the Crown. The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) would have been an effective Minister of the Crown. He is an enjoyable man, a man who has the ability of convincing a person after he has gone through a time of rough waters in a small boat that he has really been on a short ride in a very pleasant craft. He has just described for the House the air of reasonableness surrounding this Bill. He has described the consideration, consultation, care and attention that has been exhibited by the Government with respect to this Bill. I cannot help but chuckle.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud), the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and I moved numerous motions in many different ways designed to have Clause 4 withdrawn from Bill C-75, the former title of the current Bill. Each and every motion was defeated, though not by the Chairman, being
the neutral person he is, the wise and able arbitrator of the Transport Committee. He did not speak, express himself or indicate where he stood. However, each and every attempt to withdraw Clause 4 was defeated by the Conservative majority. I know that if the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants had been an active participant rather than a neutral Chairman, this colossal mistake and delayed awakening to reality would never have occurred because he would have spoken as clearly, intelligently, persuasively and eloquently as he has today about-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) was the Chairman of the legislative committee. The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants was a member of that Conservative majority.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The point is well taken.

Madam Speaker, I would simply point out that there is a generous side to my nature. There is a deep and abiding kindness in me that prevented me from pointing out that the Hon. Member was a voting member of that committee that defeated motions designed to do away with Clause 4. I thought that it was more of a reflection of the Hon. Member's other role as Chairman of the Transport Committee, so I was excusing him today, given that he has made such a fine introductory speech.
As it now stands, Bill C-39 is an excellent Bill. I agree with the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants on that. It is an excellent Bill in that it deals with reform of the Canada Shipping Act, reform which is long overdue. It makes regulations relevant to conditions today, and for today's shipping environment it is an excellent Bill. It does some rather intelligent things because of amendments, whether they be Liberal, NDP or Conservative amendments, that we were able to have passed as Members working together in a non-partisan way.
We were able to ensure the Gazetting of all new regulations so that those people affected by regulations would have a chance to comment on them and appeal them long before they became the law of the land. That is a very important change that democratizes the power of Cabinet to make changes by Order in Council without coming to the House. We were able to ensure that the many hundreds of thousands of Canada's pleasure craft were not caught up in bureaucratic red tape by exempting them where it was appropriate. Of course, there were dramatic increases in the pollution fines that had been in place in the old Bill.
It is important to note that while the introduction of this Bill without the dreaded Clause 4 would be a major recognition of the difficulty of the shipping industry in Canada, and particularly the St. Lawrence Seaway system, the committee has been responsible for providing for some very severe penalties to be imposed on those shippers who pollute, notwithstanding their
March 2, 1987

ability to pay under the user-pay clause that was withdrawn in recognition of that difficulty. We increased dramatically and severely the fine for those shippers who would pollute the Canadian environment. There has been an increase from $100,000 to $250,000 for the discharge of pollutants. There will be fines of $200,000 for offences under pollution law committed by persons or ships. There will be fines of $10,000 for failing to comply with pollution officers. I think these are very important changes.
I said that the Bill was an excellent Bill insofar as it deals with the subject matter that exists in it. It is a great shame that this Bill does not deal with the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Ocean Ranger disaster. Every Hon. Member will recall that horrific day when we woke up and heard the news that 84 men had lost their lives on the Ocean Ranger, that unsinkable oil rig which went down in the wild Atlantic waters off Newfoundland. Every Hon. Member will recall the painstaking work that was done, that $15 million exercise which took over nearly three years, by the Royal Commission on the Ocean Ranger disaster. That work was done to find ways to ensure that this kind of loss of life would never happen again to the extent that it was a result of human or mechanical failure.
One of the central recommendations of that Royal Commission, a fundamental pillar of that $15 million report, was that the operation of oil-drilling rigs should be covered under the Canada Shipping Act. It was ludicrous that that kind of activity was governed by the authority of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) when every other ship or vessel, including garbage scows, had to be regulated by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). It was ludicrous that these rigs, examples of evolutionary technology operating in the most hazardous of conditions, were not covered by the Canada Shipping Act. The Royal Commission said, cover these rigs under that Act, ensure by law, not as a result of goodwill, that the masters on those vessels are properly certified and trained. We know many of the rigs operating off the East Coast have not had properly certified masters as determined by the Canada Shipping Act. Despite the fact we in this Party moved amendments, supported by the NDP, to achieve that inclusion under the Act, despite the fact that I know every member of the committee, even those of the Conservative Party, realized the wisdom of the Royal Commission recommendation, no such provision can be found in Bill C-39.
No one has ever given a rational explanation for that. The Hon. Member who spoke on behalf of the Government in introducing the Bill made reference to an interim measure. The Bill was debated for two years and all that could be found was an interim measure. Let every Member pray to the man above that there is not another disaster while we implement an interim measure.
Canada Shipping Act
We should have acted but what prevented us? Was it because we were not able to draft the appropriate regulations? Was it because the companies were opposed to being included under the Canada Shipping Act? Was it because the coastal provinces were opposed? Was it because the people who were going to sea and putting life and limb at risk were opposed to being included under the Act? They were not. Why was it? It was because we have this twisted mentality in Ottawa from time to time which says Ministers' Departments are empires. Every piece of regulatory machinery you can attach to your Department binds your empire and expands your status. The then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, now the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), refused to give up that power. It was a ministerial battle between the current Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who refused to give up that bit of authority because it was a reflection on her empire.
Why were we unable to ask ourselves about what was in the best interests of the men and women who work on those rigs?
Why were we unable to ask ourselves what was in the best interests of the industry? Why did ministerial ego prevent a very important amendment from being included in Bill C-39?
I raise that today, not to be sour about what I think is an otherwise good Bill but because I want the Government to know, particularly those government Members who serve on the Standing Committee on Transport, that an interim measure is not good enough.
The drive to ensure the proper regulation and protection of workers in the offshore will not be forgotten with the passage of this Bill. The impetus will not be lost today because this Bill, flawed at least in that respect, has passed. Another ten years cannot go by before we provide rational and proper regulations and protection for those who work in one of the most dangerous environments in the world, the waters of the northeast Atlantic. There should not have to be another Ocean Ranger disaster with 84 lives lost. There should not have to be another $15 million story told about that disaster. Parliamentarians have to find the backbone to override the bullying caused by departmental empire building and see that a long overdue amendment to the Bill is passed.
As I said, the withdrawal of Clause 4 is a note of recognition by the Government that you cannot simply proceed with legislation which enables the Government to raise funds in a holus-bolus manner. You cannot ask for authority to impose fees on the basis that you will tell the people concerned later on what the fees are going to be. That is the equivalent of giving someone a rifle, a bullet, and they then load the gun and pull the trigger, without knowing who that person is going to shoot at. No one in his right mind does that. You do not pass a loaded weapon to someone unless you know what he intends to use it for. Here the Government was asking for a loaded weapon in the form of a blank cheque and it would tell the industry later how it was going to use it.

March 2, 1987
Canada Shipping Act
A subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Transport has been struck to look into the problems of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The at least temporary withdrawal of Clause 4 and user-fees will cause some comfort to those operators who are part and parcel of the St. Lawrence Seaway. Elowever, that is not enough. The Seaway has two problems which the Government has to address soon, and separately from this Bill, and they need to be flagged in this debate. I read an article in The Toronto Star the other day which started off, "Canada's heartland, Ontario and Quebec, is fed by a thick vein of filth, the St. Lawrence River". That is an environmental reality we have to come to grips with. We have dealt with it in this Bill, to some extent. We have dramatically increased the fines for discharging pollutants from ships. However, we have to find a way to deal with the pollution being dumped in the river by companies who operate along its banks.
There is a second problem. Even as the Government announces it is withdrawing Clause 4 it has in the same breath said it is going to consult, and that we applaud, but it intends to come back as soon as possible with an amendment to impose user-fees. Traffic along the St. Lawrence Seaway has dropped dramatically, 40 per cent or more, over the last handful of years. At a time when Canada is pursuing a user-pay philosophy for services which have historically and traditionally been provided by the Canadian Coast Guard through navigational aids and so on, the U.S. Government is taking a different attitude. It is moving towards toll decreases. It recognizes that the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is not just another Crown corporation which has to show a profit at the end of the year. It is really an intricate part of Canada's industrial heartland. You cannot, in a ledger or bottom-line style, impose user fees on a service that is in decline and not affect the industrial strategy of the country.
I, for one, eagerly await the report of the subcommittee of the Department of Transport on the St. Lawrence Seaway to see what recommendations it will come forward with. I hope the Government is eagerly awaiting it as well and will be prepared to act. Otherwise, the system which is now in decline is not likely to survive as a major transportation artery beyond the turn of the century. That is not at all an exaggeration. The pessimist would say that the death-knell has already been rung. I do not believe it. It is up to government and Parliamentarians to act.
It was worrisome for me to note in today's Estimates that the budget of Marine Atlantic has dropped by $70 million over last year. Marine Atlantic provides a service rather than a sightseeing route by the sea of Atlantic Canada. I am talking about the ferry service. It is not the pleasant way to go out and get some salt air and see some fine scenery in Atlantic Canada. It may be for tourists, and we welcome them in droves, but for the people of Atlantic Canada, Marine Atlantic and its ferry services is the primary and, in many cases, only means of transportation.
The $70 million cut announced today in the Estimates, accompanied by dramatic rate increases over the last two years, is another unpleasant signal to the regions. It is the kind of thing which causes a gentleman whom I do not accuse of always being the most rational in the world, Premier Peckford of Newfoundland, to make noises about separatist sentiment. I have no time for those who would seek to cure the ills of their particular region, be it in the West, in Atlantic Canada or in Quebec, by raising the spectre of separatism. I have no time for that kind of talk. However, when I hear it raised I assume there is a problem. This cut-back announced today is part of the problem.
The budget of the Canadian Coast Guard has been cut by $9 million. Under the proposed Clause 4 of Bill C-75 the fishermen of Atlantic Canada run the risk of receiving a bill if they thought they were in trouble, radioed the Coast Guard, and subsequently found that they were not in trouble. They run the risk of being billed for asking for emergency help. A man in a boat on the high seas who was not sure whether or not he was going down might hesitate to ask for help because he may have to pay for asking the Government of this great marine nation to come to his aid. Clause 4 is gone, but the cutbacks were announced today in the Estimates tabled not two hours ago by the Minister responsible for the Treasury Board. That will have a negative impact on our ability to help men in trouble.
I had a very unpleasant and difficult task to perform last month. I had to go to the small community of 125 people called Bar Harbour. I had to go into a house and sit at a table with four women, all widows, who had been married to four brothers who fished one boat. They were lost off the south coast of Newfoundland adjacent to the riding of my colleague, the Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Price).
I have been in this place for seven years. We sometimes get blinded by the glare of the chandeliers, the richness of the wood paneling and the lustre of the carpet. We tend to think about the the Coast Guard only in terms of numbers. We tend to think about service only in terms of political debate and, to be very frank, scoring political points. Sometimes it takes that kind of meeting to make us realize that $9 million is more than a number, more than an adjustment to the bottom line. A decrease of $9 million in the budget of the Canada Coast Guard represents the ability of the excellent men and women who work for Canada's Coast Guard to respond to those in distress. We have again today taken away a considerable measure of the Coast Guard's ability to respond and install the navigational aids which are necessary for safe shipping. I hope the Government will reconsider this. There are many other cuts that I could talk about, many of which are considerably larger than $9 million. However, I earmark this one and hope the Government will consider withdrawing such a cut in such an essential service.

I would like to join with the Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants in congratulating all Members, including my colleague, the Member for Westmoreland Kent, and my colleagues in the New Democratic and Conservative Parties who worked on this Bill. I believe that this is a good piece of work. However, at the first opportunity it must deal with the problems of the oil and gas industry.

Speaker, today is a very significant day for back-benchers and opposition Members in this House. We have before us at third reading stage, by unanimous agreement, Bill C-39, which is the infamous Bill C-75 recycled. I say it is a good day for back-benchers because we, particularly on the opposition side, have been able to convince one of the largest Governments in the history of this country to change its approach to the very fundamental issue of cost recovery in the marine sector.
I would like to refer to the history of this Bill in a parallel action, which sets my Party apart from that of the Government on the issue of the marine sector. The Government made a conscious decision that it had to extract more money from the users of the marine service, particularly those operating within the St. Lawrence Seaway-Great Lakes waterway system. I, on the other hand, along with my colleagues, believed that we first had to examine the problems of the St. Lawrence Seaway and the marine sector to learn what was preventing them from making a buck, from keeping people employed, and from moving goods from east to west, or west to east.
To this end, as long ago as July 10, 1985 I wrote to the chairman of the Transport Committee who spoke on behalf of the Government today, requesting a full scale review of the Seaway. Later that month my colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), and I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) outlining major problems on the Seaway and asking for a comprehensive approach to be taken. The Government's response was the introduction on September 24, 1985 of Bill C-75, a Bill to amend the Canada Shipping Act, among others. That Bill contained one contentious clause. It was Clause 4 which provided the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) with the power to levy charges for Coast Guard services. Those charges could be up to 100 per cent of the actual cost of providing that service.
While those of us who deal with Bills that come before the House realize that it is not easy to receive a Bill the same day that it is tabled, 1 managed to get a copy of it before returning to Thunder Bay. Immediately upon reviewing the Bill, I knew that Clause 4 presented a severe threat to the viability of the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Seaway. This included the viability of the Port of Thunder Bay, part of which I represent, as well as other ports along the system. It was a threat to coal miners in British Columbia, potash miners in Saskatchewan and grain farmers in the West. It was a threat to end users like Ontario Hydro, farmers who use potash products and container carriers who move part way through the St. Lawrence

I want to recall my speech in the House during second reading of this Bill because one reason for Opposition to this clause was the matter of process. What I would like to see happen is for the Minister to remove voluntarily Clause 4 from the Bill and refer it and all other user fees in the marine industry to the Standing Committee on Transport so that the philosophical aspect can be dealt with. Bill, thus giving us an opportunity to examine that issue with the industry, with the users, with the workers.

All of these important steps to upgrade Canada's maritime law, which has not been upgraded for 50 years, could be in place today.
Although this Bill will pass today, it still must receive Senate approval and Royal Assent. The regulations must be written and gazetted. These important changes will not be in place for some months to come. The Government made a grave strategic error by bootlegging in Clause 4, such a fundamental philosophical clause on cost recovery, to a Bill that was designed as a technical mechanism to bring Canada into the 21st century in terms of marine law. If there is any blame for the delay in improving this Bill, it lies with the Government. I regret that government Members on the Legislative Committee were not prepared to listen to representations made to them. Unfortunately, they did as they were told and retained Clause 4, which I sincerely believe they knew was wrong.

During the last week of June, the sub-committee on the St. Lawrence Seaway held hearings in Thunder Bay. Although the hearings did not concern Bill C-75, everyone who made representations said that Clause 4 of the Bill had to go. These witnesses included the radicals, some New Democrats in Thunder Bay, the Chamber of Commerce, the Labour Council as well as two past Conservative federal candidates. They were members of City Council, they were Liberals and New Democrats. The community of Thunder Bay united in opposition to this particular clause. The community set aside philosophy and partisan politics because it realized it is so important to our survival and we have to fight against it. The community united just like other communities elsewhere along the system. Fishermen in Atlantic Canada and on the West Coast, shippers and carriers all pulled together and extraordinary lengths were gone to in order to convince the Government of the error of its ways. This was done by passing staff, aides and so on who were basically saying: "Smarten up. What you are doing is going to hurt us".
I am pleased today that we have reached the point of seeing good legislation brought in without Clause 4 tagging along. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on both the amendments recommended
March 2, 1987

by the legislative committee, as well as the amendments recently tabled by the Government.
The amendments recommended by the legislative committee fall into one of three categories, those arising from Bill C-5, those of a technical nature, and those of a policy nature.
In the first category the vast majority of these amendments are identical to those made to Bill C-5, the Canada Petroleum Resources Act. Since Bill C-6 incorporates Bill C-5 in its entirety, it is necessary to make similar amendments to Bill C-6 to ensure that the two pieces of legislation are consistent.
In the second category there are a number of amendments which are technical in nature, or which are made to ensure that the French and English versions of the Bill are in conformity.
The third category contains amendments recommended by the committee of a policy nature.
There is an amendment to Clause 142 of the Bill. This clause provides for an oil and gas committee whose main function is to review, at the request of an interest holder, any decision made by the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board. The amendment clarifies the membership of the committee by excluding any members of the board or their staff from sitting on it. This will ensure that the review committee does not include members who work for the organization whose decision is being reviewed. Otherwise, this could be perceived as the board reviewing its own decisions.
There is an amendment to Clause 152 which provides that federal, rather than provincial legislation governing industrial relations would apply to floating exploration and production structures. This reflects the agreement with the province that the intent of the legislation is not to cause any decertification of unions when an offshore structure moves from offshore Newfoundland to offshore Nova Scotia or vice versa. Without this amendment there is a risk that such decertification could occur.
The amendment to Clause 232(4) establishes a sunset provision with respect to the operation of the offshore development fund committee. The mandate of the committee is to monitor and review the implementation of the development fund. The committee would terminate three years after the last payment is disbursed from the fund. This accords with a provision in the development fund agreement which requires all records to be maintained for this same three-year period. It is advisable to maintain the committee for this three-year period, but no longer.
The final policy amendment is to Clause 236 which deals with the payment of levies by interest owners for the environmental studies research fund. Under the new regime established by Bill C-5, interest owners would be liable only for back levies applied during the two years preceding the ownership of the interest. This amendment provides a transition provision to ensure that this part of the legislation is applicable from the date when the Atlantic Accord was
Atlantic Accord
assigned. This will ensure that new interest owners, who entered into an exploration agreement between the signing of the Accord and the passage of Bill C-6, will be liable only for the two years of back levies.
I also wish to comment on eight amendments which the Government is introducing at this report stage. Four of these simply replace a reference to the Canada Oil and Gas Act with a reference to the Canada Petroleum Resources Act, the replacement legislation. This replacement legislation, Bill C-5, only received third reading by the Senate on November 6, 1986. Under legislative drafting procedures, Bill C-6 could not refer to the new Act until it had been passed by the Senate.
Three other amendments are also of a technical nature. The amendment to Clause 232(4) changes a citation to the provincial Act which had been incorrectly numbered. The amendment to Clause 239 removes a provision for the coming into force of several other clauses of this legislation. These other clauses will come into force automatically when this legislation is proclaimed. They incorporate sections of the Canada Petroleum Resources Act which has been recently proclaimed.
The third technical amendment is to Clause 233. This amendment is to ensure that the payments from the offshore development fund will be disbursed in conformity with federal government accounting practices.
The eighth amendment is of a policy nature. The amendment to Clause 16 establishes a requirement for the board to purchase liability insurance, the premium which would be paid for by the two governments. As members are aware, it is standard practice for a corporation to carry liability insurance, and to provide indemnity for its board members. However, if the Canada-Newfoundland board is unable to obtain total insurance coverage, an indemnification provision would apply. Under this provision, the two governments would indemnify the board members against any costs and amounts awarded against them, as long as the board members were acting honestly, in good faith, and within the scope of their duties.
I recommend that all Members of the House support the amendments proposed by the committee and the Government. These amendments will ensure that the legislation is technically sound, is in accordance with the Canada Petroleum Resources Act, and reflects the agreements which we have reached with the co-signer of the Atlantic Accord, the Government of Newfoundland.
In closing, I wish to thank my colleagues, the critic for the Liberal Party, and the critic for the NDP, for their cooperation in allowing the report stage of this Bill to receive quick passage.

There were two large Bills containing 200 clauses each. One was Bill C-5 and the other was Bill C-6. The first Bill went through the House and to a legislative committee. Member for Athabasca and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Shields) has stated so clearly, the amendments to Bill C-6 deserve the complete support of the House. These important amendments to this historic legislation have been given careful consideration by both the legislative committee and the Government. The amendments described by the Parliamentary Secretary strengthen this Bill by building on the spirit of co-operation and fairness that has guided the Governments of Canada and Newfoundland during the drafting of this proposed legislation. It has been two years now since the signing of the Atlantic Accord between the Government of Canada and Newfoundland. Bill C-6 will enshrine that federal-provincial agreement in law.
This legislation establishes a clear set of rules for the exploration and development of the rich petroleum resources off the shore of Newfoundland. The impediments to the development of petroleum resources off Canada's East Coast have been removed. Companies that recognize this area s resource potential can invest in its development knowing the rules of the game before risking the vast amounts of capital necessary for such a development. This legislation establishes a S300-million offshore development fund and this joint federal-provincial fund has already committed $37 million for investment in education and training of Newfoundlanders for technical jobs in the offshore.
The amendments to Bill C-6 which are before the House today will ensure that this legislation is consistent with related legislation, and specifically with Bill C-5, the Canada Petroleum Resources Act. It will ensure that Bill C-6 is fair to interest holders, workers and both levels of Government.
One of the amendments tabled today, which was recommended by the legislative committee, will ensure fair treatment to companies operating off the shore of Newfoundland. Now appeals to the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board will be reviewed by a committee comprised of persons not directly affiliated with the Board.
Another amendment recommended by the legislative committee will protect the rights of workers on floating offshore structures. This amendment provides that federal legislation governing industrial relations would apply to floating offshore structures. This reflects the agreement with the province that the intent of legislation is not to cause decertification of unions after an offshore structure has moved from offshore Newfoundland to offshore Nova Scotia or vice versa. Finally, amendments to this legislation improve the management of offshore development by ensuring that disbursements from the joint offshore development fund conform with the federal Government's accounting practices.
Bill C-6 is legislation that reflects the co-operation and good will that exists between the Governments of Canada and

TRIBUTE TO WORK OF KINSMEN FOUNDATION

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute to the Kinsmen Clubs of Saskatchewan which serve our province with dedication and distinction.
