maintopic: COMPANIES' WITHHOLDING OF SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
COMPANIES' WITHHOLDING OF SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the two largest forest products companies in B.C. have decided to withhold payment of the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber bound for the U.S. market. Today is the first day for voluntary payments. This decision represents a technical violation of the December 30 agreement between Canada and the U.S., but since Bill C-37 is before a legislative committee and will be for some time, collection of the tax is not enforceable by Revenue Canada.
As more evidence is heard by the committee studying Bill C-37 it becomes clear that the effect of the $600 million tax varies widely from operation to operation and region to region. For example, some companies are exempt while identical operations across the street are not. Some re-manufactured products are exempt while other similar products are not. Some mills must pay the tax despite the fact the raw logs come from the U.S. Some mills pay 30 to 40 times the stumpage rate paid by a similar mill in another region.
If some companies are now excusing themselves from paying this tax, then fairness must prevail and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) must advise all Canadian companies exporting to the U.S. softwood market that, at least for the moment, the wood is not legally taxable and there is no interest charged on missed payments.

Mr. Speaker, throughout 1987, the Beauce region will be celebrating its 250th anniversary, commemorating the founding of the five "seigneuries" that make up its territory. What would New France have been without the people of "New Beauce"? In fact, it is the only inland territory colonized under the French regime.
Our ancestors struggled to survive in this new land where isolation helped develop some very special traits. The people of Beauce are stubborn, inventive, creative, resourceful and hard workers. The expression "jarrets noirs" is synonymous with all these character traits.
The people of Beauce take pride in their survival, their drive and their eagerness to rise to a challenge. I represent a
courageous group of people who stand on their own two feet, and that is why our unemployment rate is four points below the national average.
Today I am proud to salute two gentlemen, the co-chairmen of the 250th anniversary festivities, Mr. Paul Vachon, former mayor of Ville Sainte-Marie de Beauce and Mr. Fabien Roy, a former Member of the House, both of whom are in our gallery today.

Mr. Speaker, last week when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) was boasting about an unprecedented federal grant of over $1 million for a court-house in his own riding, the auditors in his Department were busy preying on the farmers of western Canada who are facing the worst financial crisis in the grain industry since the 1930s and the days of R. B. Bennett.
The Keystone Agriculture Producers have responded with outrage at this harassment of farmers and re-evaluation of farm equipment and of regular commercial contracts made in 1983 and 1984. The Government is trying to extract more blood from farmers at a time when they are already reeling from low grain prices and falling land values.
Today we learned that there will be 403 more people in the Department of National Revenue in the coming year. I call upon the Minister and the Government to call off these auditors and this harassment of agricultural producers.

subtopic: CALL FOR LEGISLATION DEFINING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
CALL FOR LEGISLATION DEFINING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week we heard from a spokesperson for the Treasury Board that legislation protecting the political rights of more than 230,000 Canadians, members of Canada's Public Service, might have to wait until after the next election.
I am a member of a political Party which made a clear commitment two and one half years ago to present legislation defining and expanding the political rights of public servants. This has been discussed at length in private meetings and in public debate. I and other Members of this House have spoken on this issue, carefully reviewing and weighing the many questions it presents.

March 2, 1987
This is not a partisan issue, Mr. Speaker. It is a question of fundamental rights, a question of who should have the power to define, rescind, or extend the civil liberties of Canadian citizens. For far too long successive Governments have avoided their responsibility to deal with this issue. The time has come to discard this cumulative record of indifference, to face squarely a question fundamental to our definition of democracy. The time has come to resolve this issue, not to hide from it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S ATTEMPT TO ACQUIRE RANCH LAND FOR MILITARY PURPOSES IN ALBERTA
DEPARTMENT'S ATTEMPT TO ACQUIRE RANCH LAND FOR MILITARY PURPOSES IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a range war is raging in western Canada, not between cattlemen and sheepmen, but between cattlemen and the Department of National Defence. The Department of National Defence plans to take over some of the most valuable ranch land in Canada and is offering to pay more than twice the market value. Ranch lands nearby are selling for an average of $282 an acre while the military is offering $800 an acre for the famous OH Ranch west of Longview in southwestern Alberta.
There is something improper happening here, Mr. Speaker, since three years ago the ranchers, area residents, and conservation groups made it perfectly clear to the Government that they did not want this beautiful, pristine grazing land watershed turned into a military training ground for tanks, other armed vehicles, machine gun and hand grenade practice, and the like.
Today area ranchers, rural councillors, conservation groups, MLAs and the area's Member of Parliament oppose this military takeover. I urge the Government to find out why the military is paying such high rates for the land, to listen to the people, to respect the requests of the area's elected representatives to keep the beautiful Highwood Valley for people and ranching, and to train for war elsewhere. The Government should follow the advice urged by ranchers' placards last week in Longview which said: "Make hay-not war!"

subtopic: REQUEST THAT QUEBEC NETWORK REMAIN INTACT
REQUEST THAT QUEBEC NETWORK REMAIN INTACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, trains are dying out in Quebec and especially in Abitibi. Well before the introduction of Bill C-18 whose purpose is to update our railway system, it was already clear, from internal confidential
memos, that Canadian National had started to dismantle its workshops at Senneterre and its railway network in Quebec.
The Quebec Minister of Transport, Mr. Marc-Yvan Cote, has attacked officials of the federal Ministry of Transport, saying that as far as railway transportation is concerned, they are being manipulated by Toronto to protect Western interests.
Bill C-18 is a good Bill and its objectives were supported by Quebec. However, the wording is unacceptable, and Quebec is demanding several amendments in order to restore a measure of balance. The main areas where railway lines would be abandoned are the Gaspe, Beauce, the Eastern Townships, Abitibi-Temiscamingue and Lac-Saint-Jean.
I want to appeal to all Members of this House, Liberals, New Democrats and Conservatives from Quebec, to immediately make representations to the Minister of Transport that the railway network in Quebec should remain intact. Otherwise, it will be a disaster for our lumber, pulp and paper and mining industries.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR MEASURES TO STOP EVASION OF CANADIAN LAW
SUPPORT FOR MEASURES TO STOP EVASION OF CANADIAN LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) are to be commended for their firm action in reasserting control over our borders from those individuals who have sought to subvert Canadian immigration laws. Already, all of our points of entry are reporting a dramatic decrease of individuals wishing to circumvent standard immigration procedures by declaring themselves refugees. The Government is not acting against genuine refugees but only against those who are openly abusing Canada's compassion to peoples in need of assistance.
The rhetoric the Government has received on this issue is totally unjustified. When people are coached on how to break and evade our laws, the Government must act, for the basic foundations of our democracy are being undermined. The Ministers acted in a manner which has preserved Canada's humanitarianism as well as sending a strong message to the world that Canada will not tolerate lawbreakers in our society.

subtopic: TAKEOVER OF CADBURY SCHWEPPES IN WHITBY, ONT.
TAKEOVER OF CADBURY SCHWEPPES IN WHITBY, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, too often over the past few years this House has been advised of corporate manipulations that have resulted in the totally unnnecessary closure of plants and offices. One of these tragic events is occurring at Whitby, Ontario, where the confectionery operation of Cadbury Schweppes Canada is being taken over by William Neilson Ltd.
On the very day that this corporate takeover was announced in January, the 450 workers at this efficient plant were informed that they would be thrown out of work, many of whose seniority reaches up to 19 or 20 years.
We must deplore this callous plan and last week's decision of the Canadian Competition Tribunal to discontinue its investigation of the takeover. I call upon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to exercise his responsibility and authority under the Competition Act to order that the inquiry proceed forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, the Opposition say that the Government is living in the past. I am proud to say that this is true.
We are turning back the clock on government overspending. For the first time in over 30 years the annual federal deficit will decline three years in a row, despite the burden of paying interest on the past Liberal debt.
We have turned back the clock on high interest rates. The Bank of Canada rate has declined nearly 5 per cent. We have turned back the clock on the prime rate ten years, to 9.25 per cent.
We have turned the clock back on short-term mortgage rates by 20 years, to 7.5 per cent. We have turned back the clock on high unemployment by 2 percentage points, and have provided the kind of environment in which the small business sector has been able to create 675,000 new jobs in the past 28 months.
By any yardstick the economic policies of the Government have been successful, and we intend to turn back the clock some more to return to the days when the Government balanced its books and the days when individual Canadians could expect their initiative to be rewarded.

maintopic: PROTECTION TO BE AFFORDED BY PROPOSED POLAR CLASS 8 ICE-BREAKER
PROTECTION TO BE AFFORDED BY PROPOSED POLAR CLASS 8 ICE-BREAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Class 8 ice-breaker, construction of which ought to start soon in a West Coast shipyard, will do much to promote Canadian sovereignty in our Arctic waters. While primarily and properly a civilian vessel to be operated as part of the Canadian Coast Guard fleet, the ship will be designed to meet military specifications if it is ever to be required for such a purpose.
The vessel promotes Canadian nautical technology and will provide many-man years of employment in our shipbuilding industry. Navigation in Arctic waters will be greatly enhanced when we have the capability of keeping the Northwest Passage open year round. In addition to all of this, the ship will provide a floating scientific research platform.
With the commissioning of this vessel, Canada will take the lead in world-wide ice-breaking technology.

Mr. Speaker, we have naturally seen the speculative story which was carried by Canadian Press. I do not need to remind the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that many people can engage in speculation and that the policy of a Government is not official policy until it has been approved by a Cabinet. On the question of the debate about trade in the country, this Government believes it is very important that there be the widest possible debate based upon hard facts. That is why we have set up an extensive network of consultations with the private sector. That is why, for the first time, we have brought the provinces into the process. It is why there was consideration of this question by the Special Joint Committee of the House of Commons last summer.
In 1985 I indicated to the House that we would be prepared to have a parliamentary debate. We think that would be an
appropriate thing to do. The next meeting of First Ministers on questions of trade will be on March 10. Does the Prime Minister realize that less than 5 per cent of the films and TV drama available to our viewers is Canadian? Therefore, does the Prime Minister not recognize how fragile our cultural industries are? Will he instruct Mr. Reisman that culture is not on the balance sheet and under no circumstances can these industries be treated-
Order, order.
Speech!

speechtext: The Hon. Member has several questions. They are certainly important ones. I would ask the Hon. Member to confine her question to one question and not to draw it out overly long.

those involved in the cultural industries. I agree with her. That represents a terrible indictment of those who governed Canada for the previous 20 years.
Hear, hear!

This is the result of a Liberal policy that was completely insensitive to the cultural realities of Canada. We heard it was so bad that a leading member of the NDP asked Canadians to watch ABC when they could listen to the sterling programs of the CBC. That, too, is an indication of how far the situation has gone.
Culture is protected on this side of the House, and we are proud to do it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister cares to be partisan and play with Canadian politics. Have you directed Mr. Reisman not to negotiate with those as your bargaining chips?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have three quick comments. First, this trade negotiation is not about culture, it is about trade. Second, the Government, recognizing the legacy that we inherited from the former Government, a legacy that, as the Prime Minister has said, had severely weakened the cultural industries of this country, has already begun to act on changes in film distribution, changes with respect to book publishing, and other cultural areas. Third, the Government looks forward to the debate on trade in the House, so that we will know whether there are one, 40, or 400 different positions from the Official Opposition on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. During the election campaign two and a half years ago, the Prime Minister said that the Conservative Government was concerned about providing an effective child care program. Last November at the First Ministers' Conference the Prime Minister made the same statement, he repeated it over Christmas, and this morning when speaking to a national symposium on the family he said the following, "Canada shall have an effective national child care system".

Oral Questions
My question to the Prime Minister is this. Since nothing was found in the Budget about money allocation for such an effective child care program, will the Prime Minister confirm that in all the Estimates that are before Parliament for the first time today there is not a single new dollar reference to an effective child care program? Will the Prime Minister tell us why not?

Mr. Speaker, I thought I had addressed that in my speech this morning which dealt with the urgent requirements of Government and the Canadian people involving themselves in the quest for equality and fairness for all Canadian women. In regard to that specific point, I indicated that the Hon. Member for Lincoln in her capacity as chairperson of the task force would be bringing in a report within weeks, and it would be on the basis of that parliamentary task force with its recommendations that the Government will act, as I indicated to the First Ministers, to implement a truly national, effective, and accessible policy to benefit all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has referred to the immediate need of Canadian families. They know that they have the need, and we in this Party know that there is a need. Will the Government set aside making speeches and commit itself now to a Supplementary Estimate that could be drawn from the $300 million of unallocated funds that are found in today's Estimates in the appropriate Minister's Department? Will the Prime Minister make a commitment today to use $300 million to launch an effective child care program in this country?

Mr. Speaker, in my remarks this morning I indicated that our commitment to the establishment of a day care program was real, that the resources required to sustain it would be found even in a difficult economic climate, and that we viewed this as a priority issue to bring about fairness for Canadian women. I have given that assurance to the Premiers, and I give it again to my hon. friend with great certainty that the appropriate resources required to fund a day care program of this nature will be found by the Government of Canada and introduced.

INQUIRY WHY FUNDS ABSENT FOR CANADIAN FAMILIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows full well that when Canadian banks ran into difficulties the Government of Canada found the money. It was good for the banks in the past, but why not for Canadian families right now?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHY FUNDS ABSENT FOR CANADIAN FAMILIES
speechtext:

March 2, 1987
be diverging views concerning the use of public funds, but if we acted quickly to help Canadian farmers, we are also committed to do the same thing for Canadian women and, regardless of our financial difficulties, we will find the resosurces required to implement this kind of plan for the benefit of Canadian women.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister as well. In reference to the life threatening reality facing refugees, the Prime Minister told the country last August:
If we err, we will always err on the side of justice and on the side of compassion.
Therefore I would like to ask the Prime Minister how he can now justify recent changes which eliminate overnight the list of 18 non-deportable countries, which jeopardize people who return to those parts of the world, which drive people to protect their lives through hunger strikes, which strand families at airports, and which continue to peddle a nonexistent, non-legal, non-written agreement with the United States. How can the Prime Minister promote a chaotic system which ignores the principles of justice and compassion, two principles about which he spoke so highly only six months ago?

Mr. Speaker, our policy, straightforward, remains the same-real refugees who come to our door will be provided a haven and settled. A real refugee will never be sent back to face death or torture. However, our proud tradition was being undermined by a lot of abusers. The measures we have put in place are to detect those abusers, not to deny access to real refugees.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows the conditions facing a number of families whether they are applying from the United States or from within. However,
I return to the Prime Minister who I hope will have the leadership to address a story of human tragedy within our borders. Given the fact that the only solution to the problem is the establishment of a new, permanent and independent refugee determination system, and given that we have been promised one for three years by four different Ministers of Immigration, will the Prime Minister not rescind recent announcements which endanger legitimate refugees and allow the system to continue until legislation-

March 2, 1987

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

We know that a new system is in the process of being determined. However, in the meantime every claimant, whether in the United States or elsewhere, is entitled to that fair and open hearing and will be given that hearing.
There is no danger to the people now waiting in the United States because we have an arrangement with the Americans. Case by case that arrangement is working. Our officers, in conjunction with their INS officials, are making sure that every individual is available for that hearing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board.
Could the Minister explain to the House why the Government continues to ignore the plight of disadvantaged regions in its Estimates, and specifically, considering that only 10,000 jobs were created in the province of Quebec last year, could the Government perhaps explain why it has just cut $71 million in equalization payments to the province of Quebec for the 1987-88 financial year?

The results for the economy have been clear across the country, in all regions. I think we can say there has been a substantial reduction in the unemployment rate, that inflation has been maintained at reasonable levels, that interest rates have gone down and that among industrialized nations, this country has enjoyed a level of economic growth second only to that of Japan.

expeditiously clear away the over 12,000 non bona fide claimants as we had at our door last year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the exchange of letters and the existing agreement work out very well on a case by case basis. The applicant is or will be available for the inquiry. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Member's colleague by saying that the amounts we are spending on EPF will grow from $65 billion to over $90 billion from the last five years to the next five years. The amounts to which the provinces are entitled will go up in excess of 5 per cent, and if the Hon. Member were to check the Estimates he would see that that is one of the faster growing programs of government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. Last week the Minister rightfully condemned Charles Bronson vigilante justice but at the same time he admitted that Canadians are frustrated with the present system. Will the Minister advise the House, bearing in mind that he is the chief law officer responsible for the justice system in Canada, what he intends to do to restore the confidence of Canadians in the justice system? March 2, 1987

of crime, and other areas where I think the criminal justice system could use improvement in terms of explaining the process and the reasons judges sentence in the way they do.
Within my own area of responsibility, I look forward to receiving the sentencing commission report which should be forthcoming soon. I look forward to entering into a debate with the people of Canada and with the Hon. Member on this important issue.

subsubtopic: PAYMENT OF BONUSES TO SENIOR MANAGERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board announced today $4.5 million in bonuses to be paid out after the end of this month to "senior Public Service managers who are instrumental in the realization of person-year reductions goals and expenditure reductions". speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance and I announced a year ago that we would introduce a productivity bonus for senior management categories within the Public Service with the expressed intent of rewarding the competence and productivity of senior managers. We have done that. It is clear that the Government has now created a hierarchy of hit-men in the Public Service. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I needed a speech writer, I would know exactly where to go. However, I do not.
I must say that this productivity bonus is a recognition of an outstanding effort by an outstanding group of people. I am not ashamed to say that the senior Public Service has done an
Oral Questions
outstanding job not only in terms of job reduction but in terms of carrying out the economic policies of this Government.
Let me remind my hon. colleague that the top level of the Public Service received a pay increase of zero, the second tier received 1 per cent, and the third tier of those eligible for this bonus received 2 per cent. I think that is treating senior managers fairly and recognizing their contribution to the Government's effort to curb expenditures that were really out of control under the former Government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speechtext:
In my statement in the House on September 10, 1985 I set out the policy of the Government in respect of Canadian sovereignty in Arctic waters. I said that "The policy of the Government is to maintain the natural unity of the Canadian Arctic archipelago and to preserve Canada's sovereignty on land, sea and ice undiminished and undivided".
[ Translation]
To implement this policy, we must take appropriate steps to strengthen our actual control over the waters of the Arctic archipelago. Building an Arctic Class 8 icebreaker is a major step towards attaining this goal. A vessel that enables us to patrol Arctic waters practically year round will be the best possible instrument to affirm our sovereignty over the waters in question. We will be able to provide for both safe navigation and compliance with our laws throughout our Arctic waters. The decision to build the icebreaker is a clear sign to the world of our firm resolve to exercise our sovereignty in the Arctic. It will also put us on a line with other countries who have this type of vessel and thus provide a sound basis for our position as one of the major Arctic countries.
The construction contract will provide over 1,100 person years of employment in British Columbia's shipbuilding industry during the four years the work will take.
Other provinces will benefit through sub-contracting arrangements. We will ensure that Canadian content is as substantial as possible, and we intend to obtain major long-

In addition, Canada's arctic infrastructure and control are being strengthened in such areas as ship construction for support of northern commercial operations, aids to navigation, ice reconnaissance and forecasting, satellite communication, establishment of marine parks, political devolution and native land claims.
In the past, Canadian policy in the Arctic has been characterized by fits and starts. That will no longer do. The Government has made a firm commitment to the Arctic. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to thank my colleagues from the Liberal caucus and the NDP caucus for their co-operation in expediting this Bill, which is very important to Newfoundland and it is waiting patiently to see that it is passed.
It is with great pleasure and satisfaction that I introduce for adoption by the House on third reading Bill C-6 to implement the Atlantic Accord.
The Government of Canada seeks to establish harmonious relations with the provinces, to stimulate economic development and foster social justice from coast to coast. Every action it takes necessarily bears witness to this fundamental guiding principle of the Government. Bill C-6 is another striking example.
We believe that the country's stability and prosperity depend on each provincial Government fully carrying out its role within our political and economic framework. That is why this Bill establishes the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador as equal partners in the management of offshore oil and gas resources.
The establishment of the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Oil and Gas Board under the Accord demonstrates this recognition by assigning an equal number of representatives from each Government as well as a chairperson selected by
mutual agreement. The Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador will jointly give to the board instructions on key issues such as the rate and method of exploration and production of petroleum resources. In this manner, the two levels of Government will be able to ensure that the board is kept aware of their primary concerns. Similarly, a number of basic board decisions can be reviewed by either Government. This management system, which is based on the responsibilities and capabilities of both parties, is a model of co-operation and co-ordination, something which has been absent for a number of years.
These basic concepts also guide the Government's economic position. We believe that in order to foster economic development throughout Canada it is necessary to stimulate the economy of each province. This requires, among other things, the revival of provincial sources of revenue. Hence, in addition to a joint management system, the Government of Canada grants Newfoundland access to revenues deriving from the exploration or exploitation of offshore oil and gas resources. This sharing is possible because we consider oil and gas resources offshore Newfoundland to be the same as land resources.
As a result of this Bill, the province will participate in key resource management decisions and provincial statutes regarding resource revenues will be incorporated. These important measures are introduced pursuant to federal legislation in an area where the Government of Canada has jurisdiction. The Bill also provides for equalization payments to Newfoundland once production has reached a specified level. The purpose of these payments is to ensure that the province is not penalized, and that it will be able to benefit from the additional revenue for a period defined in Part V of the Bill.
However, we also believe that economic development must promote social justice, and that job creation is one of the best ways to bring this about. To this end, Bill C-6 establishes the $300 million Canada-Newfoundland Development Fund, three-quarters of which is funded by the Government of Canada. It allows the province to set up the socio-economic infrastructure needed to allow it to profit from offshore oil and natural gas development.
In order to establish this infrastructure, Newfoundland will undertake the construction of access roads or drilling rig manufacturing plants, and it will be prepared to provide required goods and services. It will also attend to the training of the people needed to fill the positions that will become available because of these activities. All these activities will create jobs.
In concluding, I wish to quote the Hon. Brian Peckford, Premier of Newfoundland, on the occasion of the signing of the Atlantic Accord on February 11, 1985. He stated:
this whole agreement has been accomplished recognizing our role in Confederation and our commitment to national self-sufficiency for Canada-
March 2, 1987

There is no other document in existence that so clearly establishes Newfoundland's right to have a significant say and control over such a huge resource ... Today marks a watershed in the development of Newfoundland. It signals a dramatic turning point in the economic history of this place.
His words underline in an eloquent fashion the achievement of the objectives set by the Canadian Government when it first took office. We are convinced-and Bill C-6 is further evidence of this-that by giving each province increased control over its economy, the political unity and economic prosperity of the whole country are strengthened.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak on third reading of Bill C-6, a very important piece of legislation in terms of what it can do for the Province of Newfoundland. I do not agree with a great deal of the legislation and think that it is counterproductive. However, it is important that it be passed as soon as possible.
As I said at report stage, I do not agree with the change to Clause 233 which would strike out the following words: "There is hereby appropriated for the purposes of making payments pursuant to this Part". If we just say that funds can be taken from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and there is no reference in the section to the funds actually being appropriated, the funds may not go to the Province of Newfoundland as quickly as it would like. In accordance with the spirit of the agreement between the province and the federal Government, the funds should be appropriated immediately and put into the special development fund so that they can be used, and perhaps even accumulate some interest, for the benefit of the people of Newfoundland. It is a complete change of the position and the spirit of the agreement between the two Governments.
I am also unclear about Clause 41(l)(b) which refers to the feedstock requirements of the facilities at Come-By-Chance, if the facilities were operating at capacity. What may be intended here is sufficient feedstock to service the refinery at Come-By-Chance. However, the wording is not very secure and it more or less excludes Come-By-Chance if the refinery is not operating at capacity, which would be very damaging to the Province of Newfoundland. The wording in Clause 41(l)(b) should be clarified. The federal Government should state emphatically what it means in that very important clause.
With the passage of the Bill through the House and subsequently through the other place, $225 million, as agreed by the federal Government and the Province of Newfoundland, will go to the development fund. Finally it will be available to the province to help it develop infrastructure and facilities to assist it in being ready for the time when Hibernia and other oil deposits reach the developmental stage.
I only hope that the Province of Newfoundland spends the money a lot better than did the Province of Nova Scotia. That province built roads, but they were nowhere near areas where there would be oil or gas development or any of the oil or gas coming ashore. It was used for political purposes. I request the
Atlantic Accord
Government of Newfoundland to use the money to develop infrastructure for the offshore. It is important for the people of Newfoundland that nothing happens to delay further the bringing ashore of oil reserves off the coast. I emphasize that it has been delayed enough and that the passage of the Bill will do nothing to bring on those reserves. We need resolve on the part of the federal Government to develop a fiscal regime to bring about a policy which will take major producers by the ears and say that the reserve must be developed.
The people of Newfoundland have been disappointed many times. One example would be the Churchill linerboard plant. They have suffered through the ups and downs of the refinery at Come-By-Chance, which we hope is on an up cycle and will continue in that way. They cannot wait forever to realize the potential of Hibernia and other deposits off the coast of Newfoundland.
This area has tremendous potential, and the potential is being allowed to dissipate. Many small business which were operating with the express purpose of being part of the exploration and development of Hibernia were unable to keep their businesses going and have closed their doors. As many as 200 small businesses have been lost because of the Government's delay in bringing this important resource ashore and in delaying the fiscal regime necessary to act as the cohesive force.
The most damaging aspect occurred almost a year ago when Chevron sent $500 million back to its parent company in San Francisco, stating as a reason for doing so that the indecision about Hibernia and the lack of resolve by the federal Government with regard to this important resource made it unsure of the future role of Hibernia in Canada's oil and gas sector. Rather than dealing with the uncertainty of sitting and waiting for something to happen, it sent the $500 million back to its parent company. It was very damaging because it was $500 million targeted for equity on the offshore. We are not only minus the $500 million itself, but we are also minus the borrowing leverage which the $500 million could bring. If the parent company in turn lends the subsidiary in Canada millions of dollars, it would not be the same because the parent company would be borrowing from the head office. Unfortunately the delay has caused the loss of a potential $500 million in equity.
However, the potential remains. The Avalon Basin is tremendously rich in oil and gas. Unfortunately government programs have met a drastic cut-back in exploration. The uncertainty of the Government in terms of where it is going and the importance of developing the Avalon Basin area has meant that the industry has cooled and backed away from previous intense negotiations about bringing the reserves onstream. I ask the Government to bring this matter forward.
Bill C-6 was introduced and given first reading as Bill C-94 in the previous session on February 7. At least two months later it was given second reading. It was the end of June before it went to the legislative committee along with Bill C-92 for study. Because of the co-operation of the two opposition

March 2, 1987
Atlantic Accord
Parties, Bill C-92 went through committee stage. Then Bill C-92 became Bill C-5 in the present session, was passed at report stage, given third reading, was subsequently passed in the other place, and has now become law. Because of time constraints we were unable to deal with Bill C-94, as it was then known, or Bill C-6 before us now. It went to committee not as soon as we returned but weeks later. Here we are today on March 2 dealing with report stage and third reading of the Bill.
This is a Bill that could potentially provide the Province of Newfoundland with $225 million in development funds. Months ago the Province of Newfoundland passed its companion legislation and it has been waiting for this House to pass its Bill. I think the Government has perpetrated a breach of trust. I think it is unfair to the people of Newfoundland and the Government of Newfoundland. However, it is not surprising when one considers the way the Government backed away from the potential economic value of Hibernia to the Province of Newfoundland.
I would ask the Government as I have asked it before to please proceed with Hibernia and to pass this legislation as quickly as possible, as I think the Government will do after today. I plead with the Government to get on immediately with the development of those very important oil reserves.

Madam Speaker, I have a few words to say on third reading stage of this very important Bill. Of course, I agree with the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan). The Government does have control of the agenda. I do not want the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson) to return to Newfoundland to say that either the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, who is a Liberal, or the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who is a member of the NDP, was holding up this Bill. We are not holding up the Bill. We do not have control of the parliamentary agenda. The Government could have brought this Bill before the House at any time. Now it is before us. Let us deal with it.
I have some real concerns in the back of my mind. We could be setting up a strange creature we have not examined properly over which we may not have control. That creature is this dual management of the offshore resource. I know it is a way of trying to get around the problem of giving Newfoundland control without the requirement of a constitutional amendment. The Supreme Court of Canada says that the federal Government owns the offshore, so I know what the Government is trying to do. However, I think we may have created a rather strange creature that may be difficult to control.
During the second of the two committee hearings which were held, I tried to voice my concern. As reported at page 1:93 of the committee hearing of Tuesday, November 4, 1986,
I put it this way:
Let us say as a matter of national policy the government decides it wants to change the situation fairly dramatically in Hibernia to develop it to take Canadian control over the development. This is hypothetical. Mobil does not want to go ahead with it. They have things in other parts of the world they want to do. The Government of Canada decides we have to go with Hibernia and the board sides with Mobil. How locked in are we to an independent board as opposed to national policy set by a Minister?
This question has now come up again.
D. Paul Emond of Osgoode Hall Law School wrote an article in Resources, the newsletter of the Canadian Institute of Resources Law, an eminent Calgary group. In the Resources newsletter number 12 of August 1985, Professor Emond spoke of the problem involved with control over what we are setting up. He said:
Offshore exploration activity is partly the result of massive federal subsidies. While costly, these expenditures have made good political and even economic sense. They have enabled us to learn more about the size and accessibility of frontier oil and gas. They have benefited have-not provinces such as Newfoundland. They have also benefited other Canadians, as owners of the frontier lands. How else can Canada justify paying such large subsidies for offshore exploration?
We have spent about $11 billion on offshore exploration subsidies since 1960. Professor Emond continues:
One would have expected, therefore, that the federal government would be reluctant to give up almost all of the financial benefits that development of the Newfoundland offshore might bring.
The Atlantic Accord expresses the federal interest in the Newfoundland offshore in terms of national self-sufficiency, security of supply and, to a lesser extent, Canadianization of the industry. This seriously understates the federal interest. In the past, Canadian energy policy has reflected a multiplicity of interests, including conservation, environmental protection, economic development, regional disparity, and consumer price protection.
This apparent narrowing of federal policy interest would be less disturbing if the Accord provided for periodic review and mechanisms by which it could be adjusted. But, without Newfoundland's consent, that option is not available. Indeed, if Newfoundland achieves the requisite support from other provinces, clause 64 commits the federal Government to introduce a mutually agreeable resolution into Parliament to constitutionally entrench the Accord. If that should happen, the Accord and the Board would be effectively insulated from any government review.
Professor Emond also points out in this article that the board is almost completely divorced from government policy. That is what I meant when I described this hybrid we have created. Suppose there is another energy crisis in the 1990s and we have to develop Hibernia right away. Suppose the federal Government wants to be involved in it. There may be some difficulties over that with the board.
It has been put another way by Frances Russell, a very thoughtful journalist who writes for the Winnipeg Free Press. Her column in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 17 reads in part as follows:
One sure way to achieve harmony, of course, is to give your opposite number everything he wants and more.
The Mulroney government conceded without a murmur what the Liberals had fought, at great political cost, to achieve: that Ottawa, as the government of ail Canadians, should have some access to the nation's resource wealth.
Although Ottawa's constitutional ownership rights to Newfoundland's offshore resources were upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada, the Liberals planned to give the province a minority say in management and full revenues until it became one of Confederation's "haves."
March 2, 1987

The Mulroney government went a giant step further in Carney's Atlantic Accord. It provided for joint management of the resource, with Newfoundland having the exclusive right to set royalties and with disputes between the two governments to be resolved by a panel of appointed officials.
The following is the key paragraph in the column:
Fundamental matters of state involving the national interest are to be decided, not by the national government, but by a group of bureaucrats, half of whom represent a province.
Ms. Russell goes on to say:
The Western Accord, signed with Alberta, Saskatchewan and B.C., was a complete federal rout.
The dismantling of the Liberals' National Energy Policy meant a total repudiation of Ottawa's hard-won power back to provincial capitals, and a potentially massive flow of revenue from the federal government through the provinces back to the oil companies.
If I might put it another way, Frances Russell is really asking who is speaking for Canada. I must say that I am surprised that members of the Liberal Party have not put up more of a defence of its own National Energy Program rather than succumbing so easily to some of the Tory myths about the National Energy Program. That program had faults and it had some pluses. Conservatives just do not tell the truth about it and I think the Liberals have bought those myths too easily. They should have defended the program.
Let me return to the Bill that is before us. All of us in the House want to pass the Bill in order to help Newfoundland. We want Newfoundland to become a have province and to be like some of the western provinces that have used their resources for economic growth. We all believe in that. However, I am saying that there is a little niggling doubt in the back of my mind. Professor Emond and Frances Russell talked about it as well. That doubt is that in an energy crisis when we will need a national policy for Canada, will a future Government be stymied by the fact that we have set up this hybrid, strange creature that will manage the Newfoundland offshore, a board that will either be a creature of the provincial Government or a creature unto itself, removed from government policy? You should not on principle remove bureaucrats from the control of their political masters, so that when there is a concern over national policy you can act. While I hope we do not, I am afraid we might wake up in 10 years and regret that we did not give that closer scrutiny in this Bill.
As far as I can see, there is nothing happening in oil exploration off Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. In fact, exploration has collapsed. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion review of capital investment reports that petroleum companies operating in Newfoundland, who cut their investment by 42 per cent in 1986, will pare off another 46 per cent this year. In dollar terms the investment declined from $443 million in 1985 to $356 million last year, and they anticipate a mere $270 million next year. In other words, as long as world oil prices are down and the Government does not give more grants, there is not going to be much exploration off Newfoundland. The Globe and Mail says that offshore
Atlantic Accord
exploration for oil and gas is expected to remain stagnant with only one or two rigs working off the Newfoundland coast.
While we all tried to support this Bill in that we thought it was an example of the new federal-provincial co-operation, we now know that the Premier of Newfoundland has had some fundamental differences over the fisheries question with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Ministers. We have to contrast the urgency attached by the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to speedy passage of Bill C-94 in the last session of Parliament with the lackadaisical approach by the present Minister in bringing this Bill forward. Newfoundlanders are now seeing the reality in a Government led by a Prime Minister who once said, in the course of the election campaign, that he was not afraid to inflict prosperity on Newfoundland.
In the course of committee deliberations on this Bill and Bill C-5 previously which dealt with frontier energy, concerns were expressed about encouraging balanced, sustainable, long-term regional development and the need to ensure that the development of the offshore petroleum industry in Newfoundland proceeds carefully so as not to harm the vital fishing industry on which so many Newfoundlanders depend for their livelihood. Now, however, the Prime Minister's Government has, in its own inimitable fashion, simplified matters by handing over the fishery to France. We need a regional development strategy. I was hoping the legislative committee would hold some hearings in Atlantic Canada, examine the development fund details and look at safety concerns. After all, we had the Ocean Ranger disaster involving a tragic loss of life. These rigs are going to go into Iceberg Alley, and we have not really looked at the danger there. I hoped we would look into preferential hiring of local people and the effect of development on other industries such as the forest and fishing industries of Newfoundland. I hoped we would look at Canadianization and who will benefit from it. Will it be Mobil Oil of New York or will it be Canadians? Finally, I hoped we would look at the role of Petro-Canada. Yet we did none of that. Quite frankly, the Conservative Members on the committee were not interested in examining these issues which have to be examined.
As someone who is not from Atlantic Canada, like some other speakers in this debate, I find that many of the Premiers in Atlantic Canada have sold a kind of bill of goods to the people there. "This great development is a pot of gold and you are going to be rich tomorrow". That is wrong. It is fraudulent in many ways. I know they have won elections like that, but I think politicians have to be honest with the people of Newfoundland about regional development. If I can put it as honestly as I would like to, I say to the people of Newfoundland that it is my observation that they should not forget their fishing industry. Do not forget the forest, mining and tourism industries. Do not just go for this pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Do not think that Hibernia is somehow going to be a heaven and you will have a big surplus fund like Alberta has. I hope there is development.

March 2, 1987
Atlantic Accord
I said in my speech in this House on second reading on May 26, 1986, that we need Hibernia in the 1990s. We are asleep now and we are going to have another energy crisis. Oil is a non-renewable resource and we are running out of cheap and easily obtainable oil. The National Energy Board told us we will be running out in about eight years. We will have to go to the frontier and it will cost Canadians a lot more. The price of gas could be double what it is today if we have to develop those resources. The world oil resources will then be concentrated in the Middle East, a very unstable area. We are looking at an energy crisis in the 1990s and we should wake up and realize it. That is why the development of Hibernia is important. That is why this Bill is important. It is flawed in many ways, it was a quick fix Atlantic energy Accord in the style of the Government. However, we will do our best to make it work, and that is why we are prepared to let it go through today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Price (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would much prefer to discuss some of the more positive aspects of this legislation but I will succumb to the temptation to comment on a number of statements made by members from both opposition Parties with respect to delays. The Hon. Member for Cape Breton- The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) indicated a concern over the length of time the Government took to introduce this legislation. I simply ask him where he and his Government were prior to 1984 when the Government of Newfoundland approached his Liberal Government in Ottawa to try to resolve this dispute so we could get on with development. He knows and the country knows how many times the provincial Government made those approaches and how many times it was rebuked. I would also remind the Hon. Member that within six months of taking office, this Government went to Newfoundland and signed the Atlantic Accord. For the Hon. Member's information, the legislation was introduced and debated, and it could have been passed in a timely fashion concurrent with the legislation in the province. Why did it not get through all stages of this House? Because of the delaying tactics of the Opposition, in particular the NDP.
Not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Indeed it is true. My colleague from Bonavista- Trinity-Conception sat on both legislative committees which dealt with Bill C-94 and Bill C-6. He came out of those committees time and time again in frustration expressing concern because of the delays by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).
Would the Hon. Member not allow the native people to speak in committee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am not suggesting that we should not allow the native people to speak. I am suggesting-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Price) has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. The delays were indeed unnecessary delays. I, being a member of the legislative committee on Bill C-6, do not mind saying in this House that I supported an extension of the committee sitting so that we could get on with the passage of this Bill. We indeed extended the sittings on that day and got through that Bill in a timely fashion because we, as Members from the Province of Newfoundland, were concerned that this Bill not be delayed any longer. We wanted to get the development under way.
The Hon. Member talks about a lack of research on iceberg movement. Has he not heard about the fine research efforts at the Memorial University of Newfoundland? The C-CORD Foundation is a world leader in marine research. It was the same Member, incidentally who said that the Atlantic Accord was only a piece of paper. I suggest that there are people in Newfoundland who think differently.
The spirit of this legislation marks a clean break from the Ottawa-dominated policies of the previous Government. Indeed, the Atlantic Accord is a milestone in the history of federal-provincial relations in Canada. We all remember the inability of the previous Government to reach an agreement with the Province of Newfoundland on the issue of offshore oil and gas resource management and revenue sharing. There were some who said it could not be done, that Newfoundland's demand for a shared management regime based on equality was unrealistic. Not only were their demands realistic, they are now realized because of the determination of the Government to do what is morally right for the Province of Newfoundland. Together this Government and the Province of Newfoundland showed that it could be done in a way that recognized our respective roles in Confederation and our joint commitment to energy self-sufficiency for Canada.
This legislation is based on the principle of federal-provincial sharing of decisions on important issues which affect the economic and social development of a province and the country as a whole. The Atlantic Accord reflected in Bill C-6 clearly established Newfoundland's right to have a significant say and degree of control over the management of its important offshore oil and gas resources. It protects Newfoundland from the kind of arrogant and uncaring actions demonstrated by the previous Liberal administration.
The principle of joint management has been ensured by the creation of a strong, independent Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board. This legislation empowers the board to make decisions on all matters related to the management of offshore oil and gas resources. There is a provision for joint policy direction to the board by both Governments on key issues such as industrial and employment benefits, public reviews, and decisions affecting the pace and mode of exploration and development. This will ensure the board remains responsive to both Governments.
March 2, 1987

In addition, certain fundamental decisions of the board will be subject to review by both Governments. In the event that the two Governments fail to reach a consensus on a fundamental board decision, the responsibility of approval will rest with one of the two Ministers depending on whether or not Canada is self-sufficient in crude oil. This legislation will be well received by the industry. It provides a stable regime within which industry can develop valuable offshore oil and gas resources in the interests of Newfoundland and Canada as a whole.
The important issue of revenue sharing has been resolved in a way consistent with the Government's belief that provinces should play the primary role in benefiting from wealth generated by our natural resources. The sharing of offshore revenues will be the same as it is between Canada and those provinces with petroleum activities on land. In this regard, the legislation adopts Newfoundland legislation related to the establishment and collection of provincial-type resource revenues and taxes of general application. This Bill also confers important powers on the province regarding resource management. These important measures are enacted through federal legislation in an area in which the federal Government has legislative jurisdiction.
The signing of the Atlantic Accord was itself more than ample proof of our respect for the rights of both Canada and Newfoundland in the offshore. That respect is enshrined in this legislation. The first benefits of this new partnership will occur with funding from the $300 million Offshore Development Fund. This fund will be used to put in place the infrastructure necessary to ensure Newfoundland receives maximum benefits from future petroleum development. The Newfoundland Government has shown foresight in its first proposals for projects under the fund. Already approximately $37 million has been committed to projects related to education and training. Through projects such as these, Newfoundlanders will be qualified and ready for the many jobs resulting from development of offshore oil and gas resources.
Bill C-6 provides protection for the Newfoundland economy by ensuring there will not be a dollar-for-dollar loss in equalization payments when the revenues begin to flow into the provincial treasury. Additionally, this legislation continues an oil spill compensation regime which, with respect to absolute liability for oil spill damages and debris, requires the oil industry to provide financial security. The new legislation includes the formation of a committee with representatives from both Governments and the petroleum and fishing industries. This committee will be required to review and monitor the effectiveness of the compensation regime.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I wish to say once again how proud I am of the achievements of the Government and the Government of Newfoundland which are reflected in this Bill. 1 am confident it will benefit future generations of Newfoundlanders as well as other Canadians. With this law we show all of Canada that the principles of social justice can be achieved through federal-provincial co-operation in a way which
Atlantic Accord
strengthens our country and ensures better lives for all Canadians by the sharing of responsibility and the wealth of our bountiful resources. On behalf of the House, I would like to thank the committee for its contribution in the study of this Bill. The proposed legislation deserves the unanimous support of the House and I ask all Members to support it accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I will not be very long. For just a moment I will refer to the last statement of the Hon. Member. He has called upon all Members of the House to support this legislation. I can assure him that I will say no to the passage of the legislation, but I will not hold it up, simply because I cannot.
While I have 20 minutes in which to speak, it may only take five minutes to explain why I do not like this legislation. The Bill gives the Newfoundland Government substantial funds immediately upon its passage, but I believe it will go down in Newfoundland history as being the biggest sell-out in the Province of Newfoundland, far surpassing the agreement made on the upper Churchill in Labrador that is sometimes referred to by politicians in Newfoundland and Ottawa.
It is the biggest sell-out in Newfoundland history because of a clause in the Bill that was briefly alluded to by some other Members. According to that clause, no new industry can be built in Newfoundland using offshore oil from Newfoundland unless every industry is fed by that oil in other provinces in eastern Canada. Not one petrochemical industry can be built in Newfoundland in order to utilize offshore oil unless the Irving refinery in Saint John, New Brunswick is satisfied, unless the Point Tupper refinery is reopened in Nova Scotia, and unless the petrochemical industry in Dartmouth and Halifax is satisfied.
The Newfoundland Bill that is the same as this Bill was passed unanimously by all Parties in the Newfoundland Legislature. It means that for all time petroleum resources taken from the offshore cannot be used to construct new industrial capacity in the poorer Province of Newfoundland.
Perhaps the only contribution I may make today is to put that proof on the record so that sometime in 20 or 30 years when there is a big row in Newfoundland about the big sell-out that took place in 1987, people may look back and say that at least it was pointed out in the House and is in the official record. I refer to Clause 41(1) under Regional Security of Supply. That clause states that the delivery of petroleum from the offshore in Newfoundland will go first to:
(a) the end use consumption and feedstock requirements of industrial facilities
that are in place in the Province on the day of the coming into force of this
Act;
The clause mentions industrial facilities, but the only other refinery that was open in Newfoundland, other than Come-By-Chance, was torn down two years ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Build her up.

March 2, 1987
Atlantic Accord

The Parliamentary Secretary says to build her up. That cannot be done because it is not allowed after this Bill is passed.
Clause 41 (1 )(b) states:
The feedstock requirements of the refining facilities at Come-By-Chance on the day of the coming-into-force of this Act or any refining facility constructed in the Province to replace those facilities;
The facilities at Come-By-Chance are the only ones in existence in Newfoundland. Those two subclauses are not required. Those facilities are not operating at capacity, which is 100,000 barrels a day. They never operated at capacity and never will. Subclause (b) concludes "-or any refining facility constructed in the province to replace those facilities". Therein you are guaranteed 100,000 barrels of oil a day from the offshore for Newfoundland. The clause goes on to state:
-or (c) the feedstock requirements of any refining facility located in the province that was not in place on the coming-into-force of this Act, other than a facility referred to in paragraph (b)-
Which is the facility at Come-By-Chance. It goes on to say where:
-the feedstock requirements required to satisfy the demand of industrial capacity, on the day of the coming-into-force of this Act, in the Provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Islandhave been met.
The Bill refers to existing industrial capacity in those three provinces on the day of coming into force of this Act. There is no industrial capacity in the Province of Newfoundland that wishes to use offshore oil. Vet Come-By-Chance is guaranteed
100,000	barrels a day. Yet in the same clause the Irving refinery in New Brunswick is guaranteed capacity which is about 290,000 barrels a day. It is operating at 40 per cent to 45 per cent capacity. It guarantees the refining capacity of Nova Scotia on the day of the coming into force of this Act.
Then there is Newfoundland, which is far behind, with no industrial requirements at all for offshore oil. There are no mothballed refineries in Newfoundland, no refineries operating on oil from Venezuela like others in Atlantic Canada, and no refineries operating at half capacity. This Bill stipulates that for all time offshore oil from Newfoundland cannot be used to construct any new industries there because it does not have those industrial requirements on the day of the coming into force of this Act. I was law clerk in the provincial Legislature of Newfoundland for three years. I know Newfoundland legislation probably better than anyone in this Chamber and perhaps am only matched by the Member for St. John's West, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). I taught him when he was new to politics, and I suggest it is obvious that I taught him very well. He knows almost as much as I know about Newfoundland legislation. I do not know of any other piece of legislation in the Newfoundland Legislature that is so glaring in intent to do harm to the industrial future of Newfoundland than this legislation.
It states that for all time offshore oil off Newfoundland cannot be used to construct a petrochemical industry or anything other than what is presently at Come-By-Chance,
which is really not operating to any capacity today. It is hard to believe that the legislation could be worse, but when one reads further, one sees that it refers to the time when there is a shortfall of petroleum deliveries in the province. This is after Nova Scotia is satisfied, after Prince Edward Island is satisfied and after New Brunswick is satisfied. Once everyone is satisfied and all the refineries of the Maritimes are blocked with oil, the Minister from Newfoundland might declare a shortfall in petroleum deliveries in that province. We are only talking about Newfoundland. The province gets the first option to acquire on commercial terms, protecting the big multinational oil companies, petroleum produced in the offshore area, unless-u-n-l-e-s-s-a sales contract with respect to the petroleum has been entered into prior to the giving of the notice.
In other words, not only is Newfoundland relegated to the position of being less than every other province on the eastern seaboard, but it is now relegated to the position of being less than the multinational oil companies which are drilling for the oil. Would it not be silly for a company to drill on Hibernia if it were not guaranteed a contract for sale of the oil? Why else would it drill? What Clause 41(2) does-as if Clause 41(1) were not bad enough-is to tell the oil companies that if they have a contract, they do not have to give it to anyone. If they have a contract in Venezuela, in the United States, in England or in France, they can take the oil to those countries. If Saudi Arabia wants to buy the oil, it can be given to them. They do not have to supply Newfoundland with anything. That is why I say that this is the biggest sell-out in Newfoundland history that I know of.
Imagine what would happen to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister if he stood in this Chamber and introduced a Bill which provided that oil found in the Province of Alberta from this time forth must go to satisfy the existing industrial capacity of Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec. Imagine if it would not be allowed to be used in Alberta to construct a petro-chemical complex. A separation would take place. Confederation would be no more. Alberta would not be a part of Confederation any longer. I know the Hon. Member is from Fort McMurray because there are a lot of Newfoundlanders up in Fort McMurray and when they have problems they have to telephone his office, so I know him fairly well. If the Hon. Member stood in this Chamber and supported such a Bill which told the people of Alberta that their oil can no longer be used to build a petro-chemical complex or oil refinery in Alberta, that it must be sent to Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec, he would not be allowed back into Calgary airport. Madam Speaker, Bill C-6 is supposed to give Newfoundland the same kind of control over its resources on land and in the sea around Newfoundland as the other provinces have who are land-locked. Madam Speaker, with respect to the question of the resource being treated the same as if it were on land, there is in this Bill a section called The Security of Regional Supply. The question raised by the Hon. Member concerning the piece of territory which is off the coast of Newfoundland, in which St. Pierre and Miquelon is in the middle, and where we presently have a dispute, I would say that if any constitutional experts were sitting down and examining the position of the federal Government, they would think that the first thing which should be done is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) should be removed from his position.

and Miquelon when one looks at international law. France was in just the opposite position with respect to the Channel Islands where another country was claiming an extended zone. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to introduce the third reading of Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act. As the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) explained when appearing before the legislative committee that examined this Bill, it costs money to employ people to manage the radio frequency spectrum.
Most spectrum users have been contributing towards the cost of this service for years through their radio licence fees. However, federal and provincial departments as well as Crown corporations and Government agencies have never paid for a
March 2, 1987

Radio Act
service that ensures they can use their radio equipment interference-free.
These agencies have always been exempted from paying fees, pursuant to sub-section 2(2) regarding Her Majesty in right of Canada and each province. Currently, costs are paid for from the general tax revenues. In other words, not only have hundreds of thousands of licensees been contributing to these costs for years by paying their own fees but they also pay for those who do not through their individual and corporate income tax.
To provide for sensible and prudent administration of a vital resource, it is only fair to have the cost of such administration shared as widely as possible. We all tend to be more appreciative of what we pay for. Even if the fee is not considerable, the fact that there is one tends to enhance our interest in the service provided.
Madam Speaker, this would seem to be a very straightforward Bill. We heard a number of witnesses who said they were in favour of the Bill because it provided for a measure of fairness in paying for license fees, and there were of course other witnesses who will now have to pay license fees and who did not agree. There was one point which gave rise to quite a bit of discussion and which unfortunately resulted from a misunderstanding about the scope of this Bill. I am referring to fees collected for municipal radio licenses. These fees will not be increased as of April 1, 1987 as provided under Bill C-3, because the Bill does not affect fees for municipal radio licenses. The cause of all the confusion goes back to June 1986, when it was announced that preferential treatment for users of municipal radio services would come to an end. Municipal radio licensees were advised they would have to pay the same fees as private sector users. This proposal was part of a plan to apply the user-pay principle to all users of the radio frequency spectrum, as part of the Government's public finance administration program. The proposal was to become effective, as I said before, on April 1 and would have meant an increase in fees for most municipal radio licensees.
However, on January 21, 1987, the Minister advised all Members that these particular radio licence fees would not be increased. There will be no change, so that municipalities will continue to enjoy their preferential treatment. Madam Speaker, I think that is the essence of the Bill, and I would ask the House to adopt this legislation because we would like to see it become effective as of April 1, in order to establish an equitable system that will apply to all radio frequency users.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act. Although this Bill is only a few lines in length it will have important financial consequences for those affected by it. The Bill, if passed, will have ramifications for those government institutions which utilize radio frequencies for communication purposes.
At present, the federal Department of Communications is charged with the responsibility of setting the rules for those who wish to use the radio spectrum in Canada for purposes other than broadcasting to the general public. The Department regulates these users by giving each of them a licence to operate at a certain frequency, at a certain power and at a certain place so that there is no interference in using the spectrum. In short, the Department of Communications is concerned with spectrum management at the local, provincial, national and international levels when spectrum service has to be negotiated.
Bill C-3 establishes a user-pay principle in the field of radio spectrum. Current provisions of the Radio Act exempt federal and provincial Governments, government Departments and agencies and certain Crown corporations from paying any radio licence fees to the Department of Communications. However, Bill C-3 will remove this exemption. As a result, provincial and federal government Departments and agencies will pay the same licence fees as would be charged to a user in the private sector. The Government calls this equity. The Government calls this fair usage. I say that it is just a transfer of burden from the federal taxpayer to the provincial taxpayer and that it has rather serious consequences.
The Radio Common Carriers Association of Canada informed the Legislative Committee on Bill C-3 that one positive feature of charging government Departments for radio licences is that those Departments may be forced to reconsider whether or not they really need to occupy a radio frequency. They stated that if one has to pay for something, then one has to take a look at what one is getting. I do not know that that is a good enough reason for having to take such a broad sweep at this area, including every agency and all provincial users, into the wide net that is being conceived by this Bill.
If one looks at the theory that charging an entity for a service which has previously been provided for free may force that entity to reconsider the need for the service in the first place, it is possible that some government agencies which currently hold licences, but make minimal use of radio frequencies, may decide to surrender them. As a result, a number of frequencies may be freed up for other users. If there is good management, that should have happened in the first place. Our provincial Governments are as capable and as concerned with good policy and management as is the federal Government.
