speechtext:
that Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for farm products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise today to propose Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for farm products. For many years in the House I have said that the number one industry in Canada is agriculture, the production of food for Canadian people and other people around the world. I also believe that when the farmer is better off we are all better off. When the farmer is better off there is more money for the creation of jobs for young people in the towns and cities of Canada. We must do whatever we can to support the farmer who is going through some difficult times.
In essence, this particular Bill proposes the establishment of a floor price for agricultural products that has some reflection in the cost of production and a decent return for farmers. This Bill is proposing that, like workers who have a trade union or businessmen and professionals and their associations, farmers should have some guarantee that the price they receive will support them and their families in the production of food.
This Bill specifically deals with wheat, oats, and barley which are now marketed through the Canadian Wheat Board. It also deals with pork and beef. There is no marketing board for those two products. This Bill would establish a price that would reflect parity for what a farmer receives for grain with the costs of production and a decent return for his product. This applies only to domestic human consumption, because we can set a higher Canadian price without violating the GATT rules when dealing with the Canadian consumer, particularly in the case of these grains, because we do have the selling agency, the Canadian Wheat Board. That agency is the sole selling agency for Canadian grain. Therefore, we can have a domestic price different from the international price. Presently there is a $7 domestic price, while the international price is $3 to $3.50 a bushel. There is no technical difficulty in having a parity price for grain domestically consumed. We are talking here of about 9 or 10 per cent of the grain produced by our farmers. I believe that that can and should be done as soon as possible.
Some people ask what the cost of production is. We all know that the cost of production varies region to region, province to province, and product to product. There are cost of production formula for a number of commodities such as milk, with the milk marketing agencies; turkeys, chickens, and for other commodities. It is not impossible to devise an average cost of production formula that is relevant to grain producers, as we have one for other producers. So that can be done.
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
The second part of this Bill deals with pork and beef. That is a little more complicated because we do not have a national beef marketing board or pork marketing board. This Bill suggests that there should be marketing commissions in these two areas to lay the ground work for a parity pricing system. I strongly believe in economic democracy and political democracy. I propose in this Bill that we should only have these marketing agencies and commissions if the farmers choose to follow this particular route. In other words, if the beef producers wish to establish a national marketing board, that is their prerogative. If they choose not to, that is also their prerogative. If the farmers choose not to follow that route, we cannot have a different Canadian price, or a price based on the costs of production which are different from the international price. That would be a violation of GATT rules. That is why I put it in this manner. The same thing pertains to hog producers. If they wish to establish a national hog marketing agency, then we can do so, but only if they vote in a majority to follow that direction. If they do, we could then have a different Canadian price that is higher or lower than the international price without violating international trading rules. Those are the points that I wish to make on these particular products.
The third point that I wish to make is that this Bill deals with wheat, oats, barley, hogs, and beef, but it could be amended to include other products. I have received representation from corn growers in Ontario, and from soybean producers. They would like to have some marketing mechanism where their price is in accordance with a reflection of the cost of production and a decent return, and where they too would have a floor price or a guaranteed price for the commodity they are producing for the people of Canada.
The fourth point I wish to make, which may be of particular interest to my friend from Lethbridge, is that this Bill does not provide a subsidy. This Bill would take the higher price out of the market-place. I believe that, as a first priority, the farmers do not wish to have a subsidy from the taxpayer or the federal-provincial Governments. What the farmers want is a fair share from the Canadian market-place. If it costs $7, $9, $10, or $12 to produce a bushel of wheat with a decent return, then the people of Canada should be paying that price for products manufactured or produced from that bushel of wheat. Indeed, if those products are too expensive for low income people, then the federal or provincial Government should devise a plan where there is a subsidized price for that loaf of bread, litre of milk, or whatever the commodity may be. It should not be the farmer who subsidizes the consumer. If there is need of a subsidy, then it should be the Government that subsidizes the consumers who need that particular subsidization.
I make it very clear that this Bill would take the increased price from the market-place and not as a subsidy to the farmers.
The last point I wish to make is that this Bill does not deal with international pricing. For many commodities, for example, western wheat, the majority of our sales are made to

March 2, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
countries around the world. Under the regulations of the House of Commons, as a private Member I cannot produce a Bill that would call for a subsidy or a deficiency payment. That is an expenditure of public money, and in accordance with the rules I cannot do that. That is why this Bill is drafted only to provide a parity price for the food domestically consumed in this country.
On the other hand, I do believe that we will need a large deficiency payment for grain farmers for the following couple of years because of low international prices. Even with the billion dollars last year which worked out to 48 cents a bushel of wheat, the farmer is fortunate if he produces the best quality grain and has the correct weather to produce that grain to receive $3.50 a bushel for that grain. On the other hand, the Americans who are growing grain a few miles south of the border of Saskatchewan in Montana or North Dakota are guaranteed a floor price of $4.80 U.S. a bushel of grain. This converts to $6 Canadian a bushel for grain. It is not fair for Americans to receive $6 a bushel and Canadians to receive $3.50 a bushel. That cannot be covered by this Bill because of the regulations of the House.
The last point I wish to make is that many people say there is a surplus of food in the world. There is no surplus of food. People are dying of starvation. The problem is the distribution system for the food, and helping poorer countries afford to buy food from Canada.
This is a votable motion and I request that Members vote freely and support an idea that would provide farmers with a basic floor price based on the cost of production, and a decent profit for the work put into producing food for the people of Canada. That is not too much to ask. I hope that my colleagues in all Parties will support this particular idea.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for agricultural products. It especially zeroes in on the idea of having a parity price or a cost of production price related to wheat used for human consumption in Canada. It also provides for the establishment of commissions for the marketing of beef and pork. In the current national farm products marketing legislation those two commodities are not named. However, they would be included if this Bill were passed and adopted by the House.
I think it is important to take this opportunity to call the attention of the nation to the urgent problems facing Canadian agriculture. That urgency was brought home to all Canadians during the last 12 months, especially because of the United States Farm Bill. It has cost our grain producing industry some $2 billion to $3 billion and has resulted in a drop of some 10 per cent to 20 per cent in direct farm incomes without assistance in western Canada, as the Hon. Member outlined.
Recently I had the opportunity to look at the impact of low commodity prices which the Bill seeks to alter, at least for
commodities consumed domestically, especially hogs, beef, and wheat. During the past 12 months we have seen a drop of 6.9 per cent or over $7 billion in the value of farm land. In the period from 1984 to 1986 we saw a drop of some 15 per cent in farm values across the board. In some areas of southwestern Ontario and western Canada those figures are minimum. They have experienced losses which may be two times or three times those averages. For well established farmers with 100 per cent equity it is not as urgent a problem as it is for young farmers. If we take away some $17 billion worth of farm asset value across the country, obviously we are taking away equity from many young farmers who are starting out or have been in the industry for the last four years or five years or even eight years or ten years. All they are left with is debt, and in many commodities the income is not adequate to service that debt.
Let us take a look at the Farm Credit Corporation figures. They are simply devastating. In the last 12 months alone,
18.000	of the 75,000 FCC loans were in arrears. The amount of money which is due, payable, and overdue has risen from $260 million as at January 1, 1986 to some $377 million as at January 1, 1987. Even more disturbing is the fact that these
18.000	FCC loans have been in arrears for more than two years. Experience has shown that when loans are in arrears for more than two years, it is almost impossible or extremely difficult for farmers to recoup. As at January there were some 2,600 applications before farm debt review boards. During the coming year thousands of young farmers will be facing a most difficult, painful, and terrible experience. The Bill before us really addresses the farm income problem, which is a major factor.
Let us look at the last Budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He went into great detail about the $1 billion Special Canadian Grains Program announced by the Government in Saskatchewan during the election campaign. However, he did not make any commitment on how much the Government would provide under that program for the coming year. Farmers need to know whether the Government of Canada will stand behind them in the new crop year starting August 1, especially as it relates to grains in the western part of the country and throughout the Canadian agricultural community. If we look at the Budget we see no new commitments for the farm debt crisis. No new money was committed in that regard.
As a matter of fact the western agricultural caucus of the Liberal Party held hearings last week in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton, and Vancouver. It was painfully apparent to the various agricultural groups which made presentations to our caucus that the Government had made no new commitments in the Budget with regard to the farm debt crisis or to the exact amount that would be provided for the new crop year.
According to the Estimates tabled today, the Department of Agriculture has had a reduction in staff of some 275 people. ARDA has been cut back from $21.9 million to $13.5 million. Research has been cut back from $240 million last year to $220 million this year. We see no indication in the Estimates
March 2, 1987

of how much will be paid out under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, to which farmers contributed a third and the Government of Canada contributed two-thirds. There was no commitment in the Estimates or in the Budget in terms of what assistance will be provided.
I should like to refer to what really concerns farmers most. This Bill talks about utilizing the mechanism of national marketing boards and agencies to try to reach a parity price or a price related to the cost of production. Nothing has caused greater concern in the controlled commodities of milk and other dairy products, feathers, poultry, eggs, and turkey than the ongoing free trade negotiations between Canada and the United States. A year ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) told me in the House that marketing boards could not be taken off the table because they had never been on the table. In a leak from the Department last week it was made very clear that everything is on the table, that when Simon Reisman sits down with Peter Murphy, all items are on the table, contrary to what the Minister said.
The part of the whole free trade negotiations that concerns me the most is the comment made by Daniel Amstutz, the American Under-Secretary of State for Agriculture, in a radio interview on CBC a week ago last Sunday. In that interview, Mr. Amstutz, the chief adviser on agriculture for the United States trade representative, made it clear that in his opinion, there would be no free trade agreement without agriculture being on the table. He wanted to have major changes to the whole supply, management and marketing boards in any agreement Canada and the United States would sign. That is why many farmers will be very concerned with those negotiations and why we need to be concerned with the Bill before us today. Under a comprehensive free trade agreement, marketing boards would clearly be out of the question as far as the Americans are concerned.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in this debate on a topic which was the subject of a set of parliamentary committee hearings. This committee toured the country during 1986 and 1 had the honour of being a part of it along with the two Hon. Members who spoke previously. Indeed, the committee was charged with the responsibility, among other things, of examining parity pricing. A number of witnesses raised the concept of parity pricing. However, given the variety of views expressed on such issues as the definition of parity pricing and its relation to the domestic price of wheat and since no consensus was reached, it was the conclusion of the committee that it would not make a recommendation with respect to parity pricing.
Virtually every group which appeared before the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat addressed the matter of parity pricing. Indeed, some individuals and organizations based their entire presentations on the concept of parity pricing and made little reference whatsoever to domestic
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
wheat. It is therefore with some surprise that I see the matter here again.
I wish to take this opportunity to quote from a few of the presentations which were made before the committee with respect to parity pricing. I recall the presentation of Mr. David Ramsay, the provincial MP from the riding of Timiskaming. He said the following:
If the main problem in agriculture today is overproduction, and I believe it is, then it is imperative that we take the initiative and formulate a strategy to deal with this problem.
I believe the concept of parity pricing is the first step that needs to be taken on the road to a comprehensive supply management system for all our commodities in this country.
Parity pricing would ensure a decent level of return on those commodities that have their prices determined by the international commodity markets. But I do feel that if any direct price supports are instituted, we must at the same time control the level of production. It would be more self-destructive in the long run if we followed the European example of high price supports without any production controls.
That was an interesting presentation made by someone who would appear to favour the five-year program which has been so successful in the Soviet Union. If memory serves me correctly, I believe this is the Member who has since bolted from the New Democrats and joined another Party in Ontario. Perhaps his conclusions would be different now.
It would be interesting to contrast what Mr. Ramsay had to say with the presentation of the Western Canadian Wheat Growers. In answer to a question concerning supply management or quotas which are inherent in this notion of parity, Mr. Esquirol said:
To answer your question on supply management or quotas-I forget the word you used-you cannot have one without the other.
I suppose if I can be a little bit bold or deviant and say that farmers like to produce, as a thoroughbred likes to run, as soon as you destroy this incentive, I think you have allowed or you have taken away the incentive or the energy and the contribution that Canadian farmers can make to this country.
I believe those are very interesting contrasting points of view which would fairly reflect the two sides of this question, a question which I hope is more one of theory than of practicality.
The fatal flaw in any sort of reference like this is the matter of cost of production. I think it was obvious from the presentations that were made to the domestic wheat committee hearings that inevitably the gravitation is toward the highest possible cost of production rather than the lowest possible cost of production, which surely should be the target. Representatives of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association correctly pointed out the problem in their presentation. They said the following:
With or without public support, commodities will not sell above a price determined in the market place. Obviously, therefore, some surplus product would have to be taken off the market and stored-until the market improved. If the market did not improve, these stored products would accumulate to overhang the market much as they do now within the EEC.
The Leader of the Alberta New Democratic Party appeared at the hearings and was asked what he thought about parity pricing. He said the following:

March 2, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
As I look around the world in many agriculture commodities, they are subsidized by government, whether you want to call it parity pricing or whatever you want to call it. It is clear that subsidies are occurring in other parts of the world. We can talk about free trade and all the rest of it, but if they are doing it we have to do the same thing to protect our own producers.
I find myself in complete agreement with the statement made by the Leader of the Alberta New Democrats. I agree with his comments and I think we all do. The problem lies with the degree of subsidization that is going on in agriculture in the rest of the world. The answer clearly is the two-track policy which our Government, of which I am proud to be a member, has embarked upon. That involves two thrusts: one domestically to protect our farmers, and the other an international thrust to deal with the problems of international pricing.
Our producers, cattlemen and grain farmers are among the most efficient in the world. They are quite capable of competing on a level playing field with producers anywhere else. They do not want parity, they do not want subsidies and they do not want government intervention. What they would like is to be left alone. They would like to get all Governments world-wide out of agriculture so that they could compete head-on with producers from other countries. Were they able to do so, I suggest that our producers would do very well. I believe they can out-produce anyone, but they cannot compete against the Treasuries of western Europe and the United States.
On the domestic side, clearly we have undertaken to assist and shall continue to do so to the extent that our Treasury and our population will allow. We in this Government have acted, and I think actions speak louder than words. The Government has put forward some good, practical programs that put cash in the pockets of Canadian farmers, not vague notions. Our farmers are being squeezed right now because of the interventions of Governments elsewhere, because of parity and because of the programs and guarantees of other countries which lead to inefficient production and which have flooded the world with over-production. The lowest common denominator of efficiency has been utilized, particularly in the Common Market, with disastrous results for our own producers.
On the international side, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has clearly been working in concert with the other grain exporting countries to do everything possible to bring an end to the grain subsidy wars we have been seeing. As well, under the Uruguay round of GATT talks, our statesmen succeeded in securing the inclusion of agriculture on the agenda for the upcoming GATT talks.
On the domestic side, the Government has done a lot of things. It has eliminated capital gains for the most part on farm lands. It has amended the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to double the level of interest-free cash advances. It has also straightened out some technical problems to enable tenants to apply for advances without the consent of landlords. We have enacted legislation rebating over 35 cents per gallon on fuel tax. In response to drought, over $150 million was paid out to western farmers. Under federal-provincial crop insurance programs which are contributed to dollar-for-dollar by the farmer and the federal Government,
large amounts have been paid out. We amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act as promised to put forward timely interim payments each spring. Last year some $859 million was paid out under that program with more to come. The $201 million shortfall in Canadian Wheat Board sales was recently covered.
Finally, we have the Canada special grains program which has paid $1 billion to Canadian grain farmers. That to some people is not enough, but the net farm income in Saskatchewan for this year was estimated to be in the area of $400 million. Saskatchewan's share under the program I just referred to is $420 million. With a stroke of the pen this Government doubled net farm income in Saskatchewan. That is timely action and I suggest that is what counts.
I would like to close by quoting from the presentation of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association to the committee which dealt with grain and parity pricing. They closed with this comment:
Let us assume for one mad moment that parity pricing were the option of choice. Canadian agriculture earns 50% of its gross farm income in export markets. Who will buy our products at the parity price? Obviously, the answer is no one so long as other nations are prepared to meet the market. Then who will pay to make up the difference? Surely not the farmer. After struggling to achieve parity pricing, he is not about to give half of it back to move half of his product into world markets. And, if the Government pays the bill, how long will we avoid a successful countervail challenge?
The entire idea of parity pricing distills down to nonsense. It is not remotely a viable policy option for Canadian agriculture. It is, in fact, a cruel hoax upon the desperate hopes and aspirations of many financially distressed farmers.
I think Canadian farmers know that this Government's programs have put a lot more cash in their pockets than the moribund policies put forward in this Private Members' Bill.

Madam
Speaker, I have always wondered what it meant to be a progressive person and a conservative person at the same time.
I often felt it was a contradiction in terms. Having listened to the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson), I am absolutely convinced that this is the case. By definition Conservatives are contradictory. He went on for some time saying he was in favour of the free market-place, we should not give out subsidies, we should not support farmers, and we should not have all these different support programs, and in the last half of his speech he listed all the ways in which Government has helped farmers. You cannot have it both ways. I suppose as long as you send only part of your speech to your constituents you can cater to whatever group you want to at that point.
I want to say how pleased I am to have an opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-221 put forward by my friend and colleague from Yorkton-Melville. You will know that the NDP has been calling for this approach to agriculture for many, many years. I do not think anyone would argue that there does not appear to be a growing crisis in the farm community. If you look at the Farm Credit Corporation books
March 2, 1987

you will find that over the last 12 months there were in excess of 18,000 farm loans in arrears, to say nothing about all the farmers who deal with other lending institutions. Of course this farm crisis has many causes, including such things as poor debt-equity ratios, the high cost of farm credit, the fact that young people cannot afford to get into farming, the increasing cost of doing business, market stability, and the ongoing problems of storage, process and marketing, as well as transportation costs. The list goes on and on. This sector of our economy is experiencing very difficult times and, as my colleague indicated, this is perhaps the most critical sector of the Canadian economy. Not only does it provide us with the very essence of life itself, food in its various forms, but it represents something which has always been Canadian, the farm and ranch. I think they stand high among the ideals and goals we have for our country. I feel we should do whatever we can to preserve the family farm and ranch.
The fundamental problem, of course, is that the prices many producers receive simply do not cover their costs. This Bill attempts to match the cost of doing business with the price the producer receives for his or her product. A lot of people came to this country from oppressive countries where a modern-type of feudalism was a reality. Large land owners, corporations or state farms dominated the agricultural landscape. People came to Canada so they could start their own farm or ranch. I suspect that unless something along the lines suggested by Bill C-221 is done we will have the 21st century version of feudalism in Canada where the corporate farm is the major food producer. I think all of us who are fortunate enough to represent the rural part of Canada see with a heavy heart every time we visit our constituency that more and more agricultural land is falling into the hands of the banks and the corporate sector. This is not good for the long-term stability of agriculture in Canada.
Granted, if we are going to ensure that our food producers receive adequate prices, it will cost Canadians in a variety of ways. Elowever, perhaps a more important question is not what it will cost to keep the family farm and ranch in business but what it will cost if we do not. What will be the cost of rural depopulation as the small towns of Canada pack up and move away? Where will all those people go? We also have to start asking ourselves whether we want to see control of our food supply concentrated in the hands of a few corporations. In the long run that would result in a food pricing cartel and significant price increases for the consumer.
When you look at the alternatives and the fact that the Governments of our competitors are helping their farm sectors in one way or another, then we have come to a time when we have to, as the old Newfoundland saying goes, fish or cut bait. We have to decide whether we are going to support the family farm and ranch or not. That is why Bill C-221 takes a step and indicates to the farm community that we are serious.
There are steps which can be taken and legislation which can be introduced to guarantee a fair return for the producer. I do not think that is unreasonable when you consider how we
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
support utilities, pipelines, port facilities and all sorts of other things which are critical to our economy. We a ; prepared to say that if it costs this much to operate that particular venture or enterprise we will have to guarantee a fair return. That is all we are saying in this Bill. If it costs x number of dollars to produce a bushel of wheat or to raise a healthy steer, then that is the price the farmer or rancher should receive in return. This Bill refers to wheat, oats and barley used for human consumption. It includes beef and pork as well. There is no reason that, if Parliament felt it could support this Bill, we could not expand it to include all food products.
In closing let me say again that I appreciate this opportunity to speak to the Bill and support the notion that this is one way in which we could act as a unified and co-operative Parliament to ensure that food production in Canada stays in the hands of family farms and ranches and does not go the way of corporate agricultural business.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as my hon. colleague, the Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson), has indicated, the matter of parity prices for farm products has been discussed in this House before as it has certainly been in my riding of Kent and around countless kitchen tables in rural Canada. The goal of the Bill put forward by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is commendable. Surely every Member of this House would agree that our farmers deserve a fair return for their investment and labour. However, I do not believe for a moment that any one Bill can ensure adequate returns for all the farmers of Canada at all times. The reality is that no single program will achieve that goal, least of all the mammoth bureaucracy proposed by Bill C-221. Surely the parity pricing experience in the United States has taught us that lesson.
For the purpose of this debate, I think it would be valuable to review the U.S. system of parity prices and its consequences. The first parity formula in the U.S. was established by the Agricultural Adjustment Act. The purpose of the Act was to "re-establish prices to farmers at a level that will give agricultural commodities a purchasing power with respect to articles that farmers buy, equivalent to the purchasing power of agricultural commodities in the base period".
This concept of equivalent purchasing power for farmers over time is quite appealing. However, in order for purchasing power to be maintained over time it must also be true that equality is reflected in the base period. Clearly, in the United States it has become apparent that there were substantial income differences in the base period. No matter what base period one uses, that is going to be true. Basically, the intended purpose of the original parity pricing Act in the U.S. was similar to the intended purpose of the Bill put forward by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville, that is, prices of farm commodities should reflect changes in the prices of the articles that farmers buy.

March 2, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
Thus, the two original parts of the U.S. parity formula were, one, prices farmers received for products they sold and, two, prices they paid for the articles they bought. Legislative changes were periodically made to the formula as inevitable problems arose. I am relating established facts and am not looking into a crystal ball.
A major new wrinkle appeared when the Commodity Credit Corporation was established in order to stabilize supplies and prices of certain farm products. The corporation, in effect, was to act as a storage agency, making loans to farmers for their products, selling what they could, and storing the rest. The loan rate was, in effect, a support price.
At first the corporation set its own loan rates to farmers. Then, in 1938 the Agricultural Adjustment Act took over and incorporated parity prices into the loan rate formula. In the case of corn, for example, the loan rates varied with the size of the corn crop. This had incredible consequences. Agricultural production in the U.S. had already been increasing faster than demand due to rapid technological advancements. The setting of price supports and percentages of parity worsened the overproduction problems considerably. As a result, huge stocks of wheat, cotton, and feed grains were accumulated by the Commodity Credit Corporation. Attempts to deal with the oversupply problem were costly to taxpayers and not entirely effective. By the 1960s emergency programs to reduce production were required. Obviously, the investment in price support programs had become very expensive.
It is also interesting to note that although costs associated with the parity formula grew dramatically, farmers were often not at the receiving end. Much of the money went to storage agencies and indirectly to construction companies for building storage space. For example, in 1958 the realized cost of the corn program was $271 million. Of that, $110 million went to the grain trade and transportation agency. That is nearly one-half.
As the U.S. experience vividly illustrates, parity prices are not suitable to the purpose of price support. Their use for this purpose has cost billions of dollars, only part of which has gone to farmers. Let us look specifically at the U.S. dairy sector. The Act which established parity pricing, and under which the Commodity Credit Corporation operates, are the basic laws under which U.S. dairy prices are supported through government offers to purchase. Manufacturing grade milk prices are supported at 75 to 90 per cent of parity.
Again, the aim of the program is to establish a parity price that will give milk the same purchasing power, in terms of things that farmers generally buy to produce farm products, as milk had during a five-year base period. The corporation tries to ensure that the support price will be reflected in the market by offering to buy butter, milk powder, and cheese at specified support prices.
Today we see the practical results of this policy: vast oversupplies of dairy products in the United States. A herd buy-out program is the United States' current expensive attempt to
deal with the oversupply. The parity policy on its own is not taking into account the demand side of the milk market in the United States which creates a serious problem in terms of farmers' individual production decisions. That is because farmers look to the level of Commodity Credit Corporation purchases in order to judge current supply and demand. They know that if purchases are high then probably supplies are too high relative to demand. They know that if purchases are low and market prices are above the support price, then supply is probably low relative to demand.
The problem with this system is that the response of dairy farmers to the changes in support prices are delayed. As you see, Madam Speaker, if prices rise as a result of an increase in the support price, farmers will increase their production, although not by much initially. Production will increase in larger amounts later until a peak is reached. Then production will increase more slowly until the stimulus of the support price has no further effect.
The policy is based on what has turned out to be an incorrect analysis of the agricultural problem in the first place. It is not simply a price problem. Production, changing technology, fluctuating input costs, and the many variables in the international market-place all come into play.
Therefore, I reiterate my earlier statement that the way to deal with the many factors that affect returns for our farmers is not by introducing one sweeping Bill as proposed by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville. Rather, the solution rests on consistent, ongoing initiatives to lower production costs and to increase the competitiveness and efficiency of our farm sector. That is, and I hope will continue to be, the policy of this Government.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to take part in this debate on Bill C-221, introduced in the House by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I can say that generally speaking, I support some of the views contained in this bill. However, I must say that although I support this bill entitled "An Act respecting parity prices for farm products", I am not convinced that it would provide parity pricing for those commodities, except for wheat of course since this bill contains a specific section about this matter.

As I was saying, Madam Speaker, in terms of red meat as proposed in the Bill before us, I still do not think that this Bill would give Canada parity pricing in the area of red meat, particularly beef and pork. The Bill addresses the question of establishing a marketing board for those two products. I do not believe it would provide parity pricing for those commodities because 1 think parity pricing or something close to it in the red meat sector would be achieved under a supply management system.
March 2, 1987

I suggest that this should be the issue being discussed today. That is the only effective means I know to arrive at anything close to parity pricing which is the relation of the cost of producing something to what it is really worth, in comparison to the same amount of time invested in other areas.
It is interesting to have this conversation today, and particularly informative to hear Conservative Members, in view of the current Canada-U.S. free trade negotiations. We know that there would be very little opportunity for supply management in any new commodities under such a free trade agreement. In fact, we would be hard pressed to maintain supply management in the areas where it already exists.
I want to draw to the attention of the House a brief that we received recently from chicken producers. They sent a very impressive memo to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in which they state very clearly that supply management is totally irreconcilable with free trade. When I hear chicken producers and the dairy farmers of Canada who have made similar presentations in the past, I am greatly concerned about the direction these negotiations are taking.
I recall the Minister of Agriculture initially saying that agriculture will not be on the bargaining table. Later, he said that if agriculture is on the table in the beginning, we can be assured that it will be removed almost immediately. These negotiations have taken place for almost a year, but there is still no talk of removing the supply managed agricultural sector from the discussions.
I recognize the good intentions of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) in his proposal to move toward parity pricing in the area of beef and pork. I favour that, but I wish pork producers in this country would be more willing to have a supply management system for hogs. They must make their own decision and, as far as I am concerned, I would not want to be party to any suggestion that would impose a forced system of supply management on hog and beef producers. There must be an agreement among the majority of producers in all provinces where there is a significant amount of production.

This is why, Madam Speaker, I should like to end my remarks by saying that I am pleased to support the Bill of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I acknowledge that this measure has been introduced in this House on several occasions in the past. As a matter of fact, about a year ago I had the opportunity to take part in the debate and offer my support. Although I am not in full agreement with the Hon. Member when I say that I do not believe his Bill would lead to parity prices for all farm products, or even for the products mentioned in the Bill itself, I do think that the intention is good and, in addition, as he suggests, we ought to promote the establishment of pork and beef marketing boards. In the case of pork there are such
The Budget
boards in a number of provinces, especially mine, and undoubtedly it is the same thing in your province, Madam Speaker.
In any event, I support this Bill. 1 do hope the House will adopt it and that we will convey two messages at the same time. First, we want to continue to protect our agricultural sector which has been so hard hit since the Conservative Government took office, if I may put it this way. Second, we should use this opportunity to send a clear message to the Ministers by telling them that we want to make sure that supply management, that quotas will be protected in the free trade negotiations between Canada and the United States. This is why I ask my colleagues on either side of the House who represent agricultural ridings, including the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), to support this Bill because it is good for my riding, for hers, and for those of other Members who represent agricultural ridings.
